A.      THE
TRAGEDIES

[1]

This case is about tragedies - a number of them.  There are the
tragedies of two boys condemned to lives of illness, incapacity and
frustration.  There are the tragedies of their respective parents, whose lives
were forever changed by the huge burden of caring for their sons.  And there is
the tragedy of seeing good people, devoted to their duties as medical
professionals or parents, caught in painful circumstances that no judgment can
resolve.

[2]

At the closing of the hearing, the Court
confided that "
This is a
very, very difficult case dealing with
fundamentally
good people on both sides.  It is going to be very difficult for me to
come to any judgment that is not going to pull at my heart a little bit
".  Those words were prophetic.

B.       pmd and the families

[3]

Pelizaeus-Merzbacher Disease ("
PMD
")
is a hereditary disease affecting the brain and spinal cord that results in
severe developmental delay, mental retardation, spasticity and incoordination.
In severe cases, it can also cause seizures and severe breathing and
nutritional problems.
[1]

[4]

One of the parties described a child born with
PMD as being a "vegetable".  After ten days of trial, the Court finds
that description to be both too harsh and too mild.  A vegetable cannot bring
joy to the hearts of parents the way a smile from their child, even their
crippled child, can, but neither will it chain them to a life of constant care,
surveillance and exasperation, coupled with huge financial burdens.

[5]

The hereditary nature of PMD is key to this
case.  It is a sex-linked disorder ("
SLD
"), also called an
"X-linked" disorder, because it affects the male "X"
chromosome.  This means that all female children in a family have a 50% chance
that they will be carriers, though in no way disabled by the illness, and that
all male children have a 50% chance that they will be ill.  And they will be
very ill.  PMD is a type of genetic Russian roulette - with very bad odds.

[6]

Plaintiffs White ("
Marcy
"
[2]
)
and Trossman ("
Andrew
"; together: the "
Trossmans
")
are the parents of "
Jacob
", a seven-year-old boy born on […],
2002 with a case of "connatal PMD", the most severe type of the
disease.  Jacob will never walk, never talk, never even sit up on his own.  His
eyesight is seriously impaired and he is totally incontinent.  He cannot swallow,
so he cannot eat.  Nutrients are pumped directly into his stomach through a
"G-Tube" inserted in his side.  Among the many pleasures of life that
he will never experience, he will never know the taste of food.

[
7
]

Two of Marcy's uncles (the "
Uncles
")
were born in the 1940's with what now appears to be PMD, although accurate
diagnosis was not available at that time.  The Uncles were the brothers of
Marcy's mother ("
Beverly
"), all children of "
Edythe
"
Sacks.
[3]
The Uncles were treated at the Royal Victoria Hospital (the "
Royal
Vic
").

[
8
]

Edythe's sister ("
Nathalie
") is
the mother of Plaintiff Liss ("
Audrey
").  Audrey, who is
therefore Beverly's cousin, gave birth to two boys with PMD, "
Corey
"
in 1970 and "
Yochai
" in 1988.  Corey's father, Franklin Carin
("
Frank
"), Audrey's first husband, plays a key role in these
proceedings.

C.       THE PROCEEDINGS

[
9
]

In the action against Dr. Watters (the "
Watters
Action
"), Audrey, Marcy and Andrew join to allege that he committed a
fault for failing to inform Audrey, Edythe and Beverly,
or anyone else in their family (the "
Sacks
Family
"), of his findings in the early 1970s
that Corey and the Uncles had an SLD that would likely be genetically
transmitted to future generations.  They further allege that, had Dr. Watters so informed them, Audrey
and Marcy would have taken steps not to have given birth to Corey and Jacob.

[
10
]

In the action, Audrey claims moral damages of
$150,000 and the Trossmans claim pecuniary and moral damages totalling some
$13,364,000.  The latter amount has been reduced pursuant to agreements among
the parties, with no admission of liability.  The final amounts are discussed
in the Damages section of this judgment.

[
11
]

In the Watters Action, Audrey is called in
Warranty by Dr. Watters for having failed to advise "
her immediate family of this serious possibility (that
they were afflicted by PMD), allowing them to eventually take the necessary
precautions concerning future conceptions particularly in view of the fact
well-known in their family that two of Mrs. Marcy White’s uncles had exhibited
similar symptoms one generation before
"
(Paragraph 25)
.  She filed no Defence in
Warranty and, thus, was precluded from making proof in her favour, other than
to challenge the evidence made by Dr. Watters and to cross-examine his
witnesses on the point.

[
12
]

In the action against the
Jewish General Hospital (the "
Jewish General
" or the "
hospital
")
and Dr. Fitch (the "
Fitch Action
"),
which was joined to the Watters Action, the Trossmans allege that Dr. Fitch
committed a fault by failing to fulfill her elementary professional duty to
disclose fully to Edythe and/or to Beverly the genetic implications of PMD to
the Sacks Family, i.e., the exact nature of the rare
hereditary condition which resulted in the deaths of the Uncles, that 50% of
any male offspring in their family have a chance of being born with PMD or a
similar disorder known as Plott’s Disease, and that 50% of the females in their
family have a chance of being carriers of this rare genetic condition
(collectively: the "
genetic implications
").  They further
allege that, had Dr. Fitch disclosed such information, it is a certainty that
Edythe or Beverly would have informed Marcy and she would have terminated any
pregnancy with a male fetus.

[
13
]

The liability of the Jewish General would arise
because it is alleged that Dr. Fitch was its employee when she committed the
fault and, as her employer, the hospital would be solidarily liable with her
under the
Civil Code of Quebec
.

[
14
]

In the Fitch Action, the Trossmans claim the
same pecuniary and moral damages as in the Watters Action.

D.      DR. WATTERS' involvement

[
15
]

Dr. Watters, a pediatric neurologist, first
became involved with Cory Carin at the Montreal Children's Hospital (the "
Childrens
")
on May 12, 1970, when the boy was about five months old.  Dr. Cohen, the
attending physician, called him in for a neurological consultation.

[
16
]

Dr. Watters examined Corey for the first time
that morning and, despite Audrey's refusal to admit it, the Court finds that he
met with Audrey and Frank shortly thereafter.  With them, he drew up a family
tree of their first-degree relatives
(Exhibit DJGH-3)
, questioning them on the
possible existence of other family members who had anything similar to Corey's
condition.  Audrey told him about two miscarriages that Nathalie had suffered
but, curiously enough, never mentioned the Uncles.

[
17
]

Corey had a stridor, a wheezing noise that his
mother likened to the braying of a donkey, caused by vocal cord paralysis.
This triggered Dr. Watters' memory of an article he had read in the
New
England Journal of Medicine
by Dr. Dwight Plott in 1964.  It described a
syndrome similar to what is now called PMD, which became known as "Plott's
Disease".  Dr. Watters included a reference to the Plott article in his
notes.

[
18
]

He told the parents of his suspicions,
testifying that he felt that "
it wasn't fair to not tell them about this more serious possible
explanation for their child's difficulties
".  He
mentioned to them that this "could" be a familial problem.

[
19
]

This was the last time he ever saw or spoke to
Audrey.

[
20
]

He re-examined Corey in the afternoon.  In his
report to Dr. Cohen
(Exhibit
GWD-9, page 3)
, he commented on Corey's stridor.  He
noted that "
such
involvement may occur as a local congenital fault or may be on a familial basis
(NEJM 1964
[4]
)
", among other possibilities.  No one was
able to give a definitive diagnosis of Corey's condition at that time.

[
21
]

Dr. Watters did not forget Corey and, about a
year after first examining him, requested that he be brought back to the
Childrens for additional analysis in order to try to arrive at a diagnosis.
There was no sure test for Plott's Disease, but by doing tests that would
eliminate other similar syndromes, he felt that he would be in a better
position to make a positive diagnosis.

[
22
]

Frank was not accompanied by Audrey when he
brought Corey to the Childrens on May 31, 1971, but he did not come alone.  He
was accompanied by Dr. Fitch, a researcher from the Jewish General specializing
in genetics.  She was present with him at the admission of Corey and witnessed
his signature on the standard Consent and Authorization Form
(Exhibit GWD-9, page 26)
.  She also attended at his admission briefing with Dr. Watters.

[
23
]

This situation was "
remarkable
" in
Dr. Watters' view for two reasons.  First, when only one parent accompanied the
child, it would almost always be the mother.  In addition, he had never had a
patient be accompanied by another doctor for such an occasion.

[
24
]

The two physicians did not know each other at
the time.  Dr. Fitch explained that she wished to ensure that Dr. Watters was
aware that the "
mother's
aunt had 2 boys w/ similar problems
", one dying
after 20 days and the other after one and a half years
(Exhibit GWD-9, page 16)
.  The
two boys in question were the Uncles.  Dr. Watters did not know this from his
initial conversation with Audrey and Frank and he found it most pertinent.

[
25
]

This exchange of information took place at
Corey's admission on May 31
st
.  Frank was present and Dr. Watters
and Dr. Fitch explained to him "
in the clearest manner possible
" the
likelihood that Corey's problem could be of a sex-linked nature, given the
Uncles' story.  They informed him that, if it were an SLD, Audrey's side of the
family was "
of primary
concern
".  Dr. Watters testified that Frank "
seemed to comprehend well
".

[
26
]

The proof indicates, however, that neither he
nor Dr. Fitch urged Frank at that meeting to communicate the information to the
Sacks Family, since no firm diagnosis had yet been made.

[
27
]

During the next two weeks at the Childrens, Dr.
Watters, now listed as the attending physician, performed a number of tests on
Corey.  At discharge on June 11
th
, the resident who signed the
discharge form
(Exhibit GWD-9,
page 6)
wrote: "
Specific diagnosis undetermined
".  However, when the biopsy results came in on July 5
th

and showed negative results for the other possible illnesses, Dr. Watters added
the notation "
PLOTT'S
DISEASE, New Engl J. Med, 271 593 1964   Hereditary sex linked laryngeal
abductor paralysis
".

[
28
]

He telephoned Frank the same day to advise him
that everything now indicated that Corey had a hereditary SLD.  In Court, Dr.
Watters stated that he told Frank that there were important implications for
Audrey, Corey and him, as well as for the Sacks Family, that it was critical
that he (Dr. Watters) speak with Audrey to explain it fully to her and that he
would agree to meet with them in his office.  He added in his testimony that he
made it clear to Frank that "
there was still much to be done
" in terms
of the Sacks Family.

[
29
]

He further testified that he did not feel it
sufficient under the circumstances to deal with a matter like this over the
telephone.  He assumed that there would be a follow-up meeting with Audrey and
Frank where he could give them more complete instructions.

[
30
]

In that telephone conversation, Frank did not mention
to Dr. Watters that he and Audrey had separated.  He told Dr. Watters that
Audrey was not able to handle such information at that time and that he would
tell her when she was better able to receive it.  Dr. Watters "
reluctantly
"
accepted this delay, judging that it was Frank's prerogative to hold off
informing her.  Frank had presented himself as a credible person and had
impressed Dr. Watters with his dedication in bringing Corey in without Audrey.
He seemed a dedicated father and Dr. Watters had no reason to doubt his good
faith with respect to the assessment of Audrey's inability to receive this type
of information – and to his undertaking to inform her at the appropriate time.

[
31
]

Dr. Watters' contact with the Carin family did
not end with that July 1971 telephone conversation.  The medical records show
that he was the attending physician for Corey during at least two subsequent
admissions to the Childrens, one in April 1972 and the other in August 1974.

[
32
]

In April 1972, Corey had been living in the Ambar
Institute since around September 1970, at age nine months.  He was brought to
the Childrens because of a medical problem.  It is not clear if Frank was
present and, not surprisingly after nearly 40 years, Dr. Watters cannot confirm
whether or not he met with Frank during that hospitalization.

[
33
]

He does confirm with reasonable certainty,
however, that he met with Frank at the time of the 1974 hospitalization, since
that occurred at Dr. Watters' request.  He wanted to do further testing on
Corey and it was Frank who signed the admission form on August 15
th
.

[
34
]

Dr. Watters testified that he had often thought
about Corey's case over the intervening two years.  He also confirms that it
was during this period that he learned that Frank and Audrey had separated.  As
well, he admitted that, at the 1974 meeting, he never broached the subject of
what steps Frank had taken to inform Audrey of the diagnosis and the genetic
implications.  He explained that he couldn't imagine that Frank would not have
told Audrey.

[
35
]

This was the last time he ever saw or spoke to
Frank.

[
36
]

The final element of Dr. Watters' involvement
with Corey is of major significance to the case.  Between their first meeting
in 1971 and some time in 1973, Drs. Watters and Fitch collaborated in the
writing of a research article published in the journal
Clinical Genetics

in 1973, entitled "
Familial laryngeal abductor paralysis and
psychomotor retardation
" (the "
Article
":
Exhibit P-6
).

E.       THE ARTICLE

[
37
]

Although undoubtedly a work of high quality that
added to the body of knowledge on a most important topic, the Article is not a
voluminous, long-term research project of the nature of a clinical trial
dealing with hundreds or thousands of subjects over a period of years.  It is a
five-page analysis of three cases: Corey and the two Uncles.  It includes a
family tree showing both Nathalie's and Edythe's children, plus Corey, as well
as Frank's side.

[
38
]

The Article describes Corey's situation in
detail and provides a brief resumé of each of the Uncles' files.  It concludes
by linking all three to the four patients that were the subject of Dr. Plott's
work with in the 1960's.  Its conclusion is to the point:

The finding that all seven patients with this syndrome are male
suggests that the gene is either a sex-linked recessive or an autosomal
dominant with male sex limitation.

[
39
]

In essence, this sentence describes the genetic
implications, albeit in an incomprehensible form for the average citizen.  In
spite of the critical importance of these conclusions to the families involved,
the proof shows no attempt by either author to discuss the matter with any
member of the Carin or Sacks families.

f.       THE OBLIGATION TO INFORM
[5]

[
40
]

In their work
La responsabilité civile
[6]
,
Baudouin and Deslauriers discuss the question of whether the doctor's duty to
inform extends to other members of the family of the patient.  They note that
the problem is complex because it pits the obligation to inform against the
obligation of confidentiality due by the doctor to his patient.  They conclude
their analysis by noting that the final word has yet to be pronounced on the
question: "
Les
solutions légales ou jurisprudentielles à ce problème restent à venir
"
[7]
.

[
41
]

As tempting as it might be to plunge deeply into
that most interesting and important ethical debate, it is not necessary to go
to the bottom of it here, particularly with respect to present-day
applications.

[
42
]

For one thing, the standards of conduct relevant
to the present cases are those of the early 1970s.  At that time in Quebec,
codes of ethics for physicians and statutory obligations of confidentiality,
including charters of rights, were for the most part but twinkles in the eyes
of regulators and legislators
[8]
.  Thus, the guidelines from which Drs. Watters and Fitch could seek
direction were mainly those stemming from their experience in the profession,
along with simple common sense.

[
43
]

It is also relevant to note that this case does
not require an analysis of the care given to a patient by a doctor.  No one
questions the high quality of the care and the insightfulness of the diagnostic
efforts of Dr. Watters with respect to Corey in the 1970s.  The only reproach
relates to a failure to inform other family members of the genetic implications
of his discovery of a hereditary SLD in the family.

[
44
]

As such, the typical gauge of a physician's
actions, the likely conduct of a prudent and diligent doctor placed in the same
circumstances
[9]
, is not the sole or even the principal measure here.  The actions
of the defendant doctors must be viewed in the context of the obligations
imposed in that period by Quebec civil law
[10]
.  Standard
practice in the profession and deontological and ethical concerns are but two
of the factors to consider and, even then, only at a second stage, as we
discuss below.

[
45
]

The final element that puts our analysis outside
any ethical debate is, quite simply, that we do not see any necessary conflict
here between the obligation of confidentiality and the duty to inform.  We
explain our reasoning behind this finding later in the judgment, as well.

[
46
]

Before attempting a detailed analysis of the
duties, it is useful to remember that one cannot avoid civil liability by the
mere fact that one acts in compliance with applicable rules, regulations or
norms
[11]
.  The same holds with respect to adopting the general practice
followed in a profession.  The Supreme Court was unequivocal on this point in
the context of a notary's duty:

The fact that a professional has followed the practice
of his or her peers may be strong evidence of reasonable and diligent conduct,
but
it is not determinative
.  If the practice is not in accordance with the
general standards of liability, i.e., that one must act in a reasonable manner,
then the professional who adheres to such a practice can be found liable,
depending on the facts of each case.
[12]

(Emphasis in the original)

[
47
]

Applying this to the medical field in 1971, the
Court finds that the opinions offered by Defendants' experts
[13]
, centering on the point that standard practice or ethical norms did
not require either doctor to do more than what was done, avoid the real issue.
They fail to take into account the duties of prudence and diligence imposed on
doctors of that day by article 1053 of the former
Civil Code
.

[
48
]

The doctor's obligation to inform is generally
analyzed with respect to providing all relevant and necessary information to
his direct patient.  However, his obligation towards third parties, as Baudouin
and Deslauriers imply
[14]
, requires further definition even today, not to mention forty years
ago.  Today, the evolution of science and changing social mores have brought
the issue to a head.

[
49
]

Over the past four decades, medicine's ability
to predict genetic dangers was developing alongside society's increasing
acceptance of birth control and abortion as means to avoid bringing seriously
handicapped children into the world.  The result of this parallel evolution now
spotlights the extent to which it is necessary, even critical, that the law
consider a new perspective on the obligation to inform.

[
50
]

That said, as mentioned earlier, we need not go
that far for the purposes of this case.  We shall deal with some of the issues,
but only those necessary - and probably not the most difficult ones.  This is,
at most, a small first step towards that new perspective.

[
51
]

We propose a two-step process in our analysis,
bearing in mind that we are speaking of the early 1970s.  We shall start by
considering the general civil law obligations of a doctor aware of the
existence of an SLD in persons who were not his patients but with whom he was
in contact.  We shall analyze to what extent did an obligation to inform exist
and, if one did, how the doctor could determine to whom it was owed.

[
52
]

If we conclude that such an obligation did
exist, we shall proceed to the second step of determining whether standard
practice or ethical norms in the profession created an exception to it, i.e.,
an obligation not to inform
[15]
.

[
53
]

In certain matters, knowledge imposes a burden.
This is one of them.

[
54
]

Article 1053 of the former civil code states
that fault can come in several forms: positive act, imprudence, neglect or want
of skill.  That fault can occur through acts of omission is uncontroversial
but, in order for that to happen, there must be some reason why the missing act
should have taken place.  The "reason why" in circumstances of this
sort will often be the obligation to inform resulting from knowledge of
particular facts.

[
55
]

The Court understands that not just any facts
would create such a duty.  They must be sufficiently important, meaning that
they are of serious enough consequence, that a reasonable person would deem
that they ought to be communicated to appropriate persons.  Where facts of that
nature are to a physician's knowledge, then an obligation to inform exists.

[
56
]

The question then arises as to whom this
obligation is owed.  Who are the "appropriate persons"?

[
57
]

It would be a thorny issue indeed to attempt to
delineate specific criteria for every case and one can do no more than suggest
general guidelines.  That said, it seems inevitable that the focus of any such
guidelines must be, on the one hand, the gravity of the illness and, on the
other, the intensity of the relationship, either existing or possible, between
the doctor and the third persons, what we call the "radius of
contact".

[
58
]

The stronger, i.e., the more direct, the
relationship, the more likely that the radius of contact is one that requires
the physician to act.  The same direct relation exists between the gravity of
the illness and the obligation to act.  Our Court of Appeal put it this way in the
context of the loss of sight:
"The
duty to warn of risk varies inversely with its rarity, but directly with its
severity"
[16]
.

[
59
]

The parties found precedent on these points in
U.S. case law.

[
60
]

In its decision in
Pate v. Threlkel
, the
Supreme Court of Florida held in 1995 that "
when the prevailing standard of care creates a duty
that is obviously for the benefit of certain identified third parties and the
physician knows of the existence of those third parties, then the physician's
duty runs to those third parties
".  This ruling
allowed the patient's children in that case to sue a doctor in medical
malpractice, because they were in "
the zone of foreseeable risk
"
of a genetically-transmitted strain of cancer
[17]
.

[
61
]

The Florida court concludes, however, that
"
in any circumstances in
which the physician has a duty to warn of a genetically transferable disease,
that duty will be satisfied by warning the patient
".
To require more, in that court's view, would be to place too heavy a burden
upon the physician
[18]
.

[
62
]

The New Jersey Appellate Court was willing to go
further in a judgment rendered the following year in an action against a doctor
for not informing the family of a father's hereditary condition leading to a
type of cancer.  In
Safer v. Pack
, that court saw
"no impediment, legal or otherwise, to
recognizing a physician's duty to warn those known to be at risk of avoidable
harm from a genetically transmissible conditions".
The court added that

"we are confident that the duty to warn of avertible risk from genetic
causes, by definition a matter of familial concern, is sufficiently narrow to
serve the interests of justice.  Further, it is appropriate … that the duty be
seen as owed not only to the patient himself but that it also 'extends beyond
the interests of a patient to members of the immediate family of the patient
who may be adversely affected by a breach of that duty'"
[19]
.

[
63
]

We prefer the approach taken in
Safer
.
In a civil law régime, the qualification adopted in
Pate
would not be
acceptable.  By dictating a rule of conduct to apply "
in any circumstances
", it fails to base the decision to warn on the judgment of the
reasonable person in the specific circumstances, and creates a
one-size-fits-all rule that does not respond to situations dealing with
illnesses of the gravity of PMD.

[
64
]

In
Safer
, on the other hand, the court
adjusts the measures to the circumstances of the case.  As with the radius of
contact guideline, the obligation to warn will be governed by what a reasonable
person would deem is necessary or appropriate, i.e., reasonable, given the
nature of the information to be communicated and the "accessibility"
of the third parties.

[
65
]

Based on general civil law principles, it seems
obvious that where a physician has personal knowledge of and some form of
contact with third persons affected by critical genetic information, he is
manifestly within a radius of contact that would impose the obligation to
inform on him, particularly where there is only a small number of third persons
involved.  What reasonable person, physician or not, would not feel the need to
warn such persons in those circumstances?

[
66
]

Turning to the second step, the effect of
standard practice or ethical norms on the obligation to inform, the Court
recognizes that a physician in the early 1970s had an obligation of
confidentiality towards a patient.  This is logical and necessary for too many
reasons to cite here.

[
67
]

That said, this obligation did not shackle the
physician to a wall of passive silence.  Even though there existed concerns
about communicating certain medical information without his patient's
permission
[20]
, that did not mean that the doctor could remain passive about the
process of obtaining that permission.

[
68
]

In the face of an illness of the gravity of PMD,
particularly given its hereditary nature, a physician at any period of time,
whether it be the 1970s or today, must be a leader, not a follower, in the
information process.  This applies no matter what obligation of confidentiality
might bind him.

[
69
]

The physician is the one who best understands
the consequences of the case for other family members.  He cannot rest until he
has done everything reasonable to ensure that his patient comprehends both the
hereditary nature of the illness and the absolute need to share the information
with other family members who might also be affected.  Failure to take the
necessary steps to that end constitutes a negligent omission and a civil fault.

[
70
]

In a scenario where the patient refuses to
permit the doctor to share the information, a major ethical dilemma arises.  In
those circumstances, the physician would have to consider whether it was
permissible to breach the obligation of confidentiality, as discussed in an
earlier footnote.  Since the process never got that far in this case, it is not
necessary to deal with that dilemma here.

[
71
]

An alternative scenario is where it would not be
necessary to divulge confidential medical information of a patient in order to
warn third parties of a genetic problem in their lives, even though the
doctor's knowledge of the problem arises in whole or in part from his treatment
of that patient.  In that situation, the Court sees no ethical obstacle to
advising the third parties of the problem.  An obstacle does not exist simply
because one might have to exercise a certain amount of discretion when speaking
with the third parties.

[
72
]

The recent doctrine seems to point in the same
direction.  Although we would go further along the road of a duty to warn than
the authors of
Éléments de responsabilité civile médicale
[21]
, the Court notes with interest their statement that "
For purposes of diagnostic investigation,
if one also suspects a genetic illness in another member of the family, there
is no problem: there is no need to breach any confidentiality in order to go
forward"
(translation)
[22]
.
The implication
that the Court sees there is that, if the doctor is aware of an existing
condition, he is not precluded from following up on it.

[
73
]

Finally on this topic, it should be noted that
the particular facts of a file can affect the intensity of the obligation to
inform.  Dr. Rosenblatt, one of Dr. Watters' experts, advised that certain
duties of a doctor can be enhanced the graver the consequences to the parties,
speaking there about the obligation to encourage the parents to share the
genetic implications with other members of the extended family.  This is
consistent with the Court of Appeal's reasoning in
Parenteau v. Drolet
,
cited above.
[23]
.

[
74
]

It is time to apply this to the facts of the
case.

G.      DR. WATTERS' FAULTS

[
75
]

The Court is of the opinion that Dr. Watters'
actions were faulty in three areas, two with respect to the Sacks Family and
one in relation to Audrey.

G.1     The failure to communicate directly with
Edythe and Beverly

[
76
]

Although the principal ground of his defence is stated as his
"
legal and statutory obligation of
confidentiality
" and on the absence of authorization from Frank or
Audrey to contact any other person about the genetic implications
[24]
, Dr. Watters'
candid and credible testimony never referred to that obligation.  Neither of the doctors even seemed to have considered it.  Dr.
Watters never mentions it as being of concern or as a factor in the way he
acted.  Dr. Fitch, who passed away prior to the trial and never testified,
freely shared advice about the Uncles with Frank and Dr. Watters, though she
had no specific permission to do that from Edythe
[25]
.

[
77
]

Dealing first with the existence of an
obligation to inform, it is appropriate to underline that Dr. Watters appears
to have been a truly talented and dedicated physician
[26]
.  He had finally
discovered what Corey and his family were up against and knew that it was a
most grievous situation for them and for the Sacks Family.

[
78
]

It is true that he had no doctor-patient
relationship with the Sacks Family, but his radius of contact with Edythe was
close indeed, particularly in light of his work on the Article.  He knew, or
could have easily ascertained, that she was alive and he could have contacted
her with little difficulty.  He also knew of Beverly's existence.  In light of
the seriousness of the genetic implications, the radius of contact between Dr.
Watters and Edythe and Beverly was such that an obligation to inform was
imposed on him with respect to the Sacks Family.

[
79
]

The Court recognizes that this view flies in the
face of the opinions of Dr. Watters' experts.

[
80
]

Dr. Rosenblatt stated before us that for Dr.
Watters to tell Edythe of the diagnosis of the Uncles would be a breach of
confidentiality towards the Carins.  When pressed, he retreated to saying that
it was, rather, "
outside
the normal way of doing things
".  He added that
Edythe "
does not have
entitlement

to be informed
" of the genetic nature of
the Uncles' illness, while admitting that he would "
prefer

that Edythe be informed
"
[27]
.

[
81
]

For reasons explained later in this judgment,
the Court disagrees with Dr. Rosenblatt on the issue of Edythe's entitlement.

[
82
]

As well, he does not declare that Dr. Watters
would have been committing a breach of his ethical duty by communicating with
Edythe or Beverly.  His report is silent on this issue and his testimony was
equivocal enough to lead the Court to conclude that he saw no real obstacle to
such an initiative.

[
83
]

In any event, the Court does not accept that
such an obstacle existed, admitting, as discussed below, that Dr. Watters might
have had to tread carefully in the manner in which he divulged the information
to them.

[
84
]

Dr. Louis Dallaire also testified as an expert
for Dr. Watters.  His main conclusion was that it is the parents'
responsibility to communicate medical information to members of the family who
might be affected.  He stated in his report that a geneticist is not allowed,
without permission, to contact other family members for the purpose of
communicating medical information to them.
[28]

[
85
]

He states at pages 2 and 5 that he had knowledge
of the Article and its conclusions and gives a brief description of its
contents, later adding that "
a scientific article does not constitute genetic counselling
"
[29]
.  What causes us to reject his analysis is what he states in the
following paragraph:

6-  The publication of Watters and Fitch must have
required a genetic study of the family, with meetings with one or both of the
families involved.  The fact of having prepared a genetic history confirms the
existence of contacts with the family and that the question of a hereditary
illness was certainly dealt with in one or several interviews.  The family
trees
(sic)
were prepared using information from the
parents who, themselves, furnished the details and certainly raised the issue
that there were other members affected in the family.
[30]

(translation)

[
86
]

This passage shows that Dr. Dallaire was not
aware of all relevant facts when he prepared his opinion and, as well, that he
based himself on incorrect assumptions, i.e., that the Sacks Family had had
meetings and other contacts with the doctors and had attended one or several
interviews on the question of hereditary illness.  More to the point, it
indicates that those steps should have been taken.  Going further, if "it
goes without saying" that something was done, as this expert clearly
believes, must the Court not deduce that, absent some exculpatory explanation,
failure to do so constitutes an error?

[
87
]

Thus, Dr. Dallaire's opinion is most revealing
and useful, but not in the way intended by Drs. Watters and Fitch.  Not only
does it undermine one of their principal arguments, but it also establishes the
commission of a fault, since nothing in the evidence even attempts to explain
away the omission(s).

[
88
]

Finally on the question of Dr. Watters' experts,
it is important to underline that neither of them attempted to opine on the
existence of a legal obligation to inform, and they were correct in excluding
that aspect.  It lies outside of their areas of expertise.

[
89
]

For his part, Dr. Watters appears not to have seen any obstacle
to his communicating with the Sacks Family.

[
90
]

To the question of whether he instructed Frank "
to tell the Sacks family (of the genetic
implications), since … they had the same exposure and the same risk
",
Dr. Watters testified in his
examination on discovery that "
I did not tell him to inform the Sacks family, but I presume, because
Doctor Fitch was involved with the Sacks family, that … she would take that
responsibility
"
[31]
.  Any concerns
over the obligation of confidentiality seemed to be far from his mind.

[
91
]

He does not try to hide behind theoretical
deontological ruminations.  He readily acknowledges that it was "
very important
"
that the Sacks family be told of the genetic implications and he does not try
to deny that he had a role to play in that.  That said, his role was not
limited to presuming that another person would carry out this vital task.
Several of the Defendants' experts confirmed that in cross-examination.

[
92
]

Unfortunately for all concerned, the particular,
and peculiar, circumstances in 1971 seem to have led him into making an
erroneous presumption or, rather, into erroneously basing his actions on an
otherwise logical presumption.  It was not illogical for him to think that Dr.
Fitch would provide genetic counselling to Edythe and her family but, given the
gravity of the issue at hand, he was not entitled to leave it at that.  He
should have followed up on the point either with Dr. Fitch or with Edythe or
Beverly, who by then was 29 years old and already the mother of two children.

[
93
]

Dr. Watters admitted that he "
did not directly ask Doctor Fitch if she
had communicated (the genetic implications) with the Sacks family
", adding that "
I don't know for certain (if anyone communicated with the Sacks
family), except to know that (Dr. Fitch) was involved with the Sacks family
because she brought that information about the Sacks family to the assessment
of Corey in 1971
"
[32]
.  This was not
enough.  At the very least, he should have confirmed with Dr. Fitch that what
needed to be done had been done.

[
94
]

He replied at trial that he did not ask Dr.
Fitch if she had informed Edythe because "
I would have had no occasion to discuss that with
(her)
".  This seems rather surprising in light of
their collaboration on the article between 1971 and 1973.

[
95
]

Coming back to the defence, all defendants limit
the debate to a possible breach of Corey's and his parents' right to
confidentiality.  In doing so, they pass over Edythe's and Beverly's right to
be informed about the implications of the Uncles' illness.  They appear to
assume that it would be impossible to impart such information without breaching
the confidentiality owed to Corey's parents.

[
96
]

The Court sees no basis for such an assumption.
Dr. Watters was squarely within the alternative scenario outlined above.  In
that light, the Court is of the same opinion as Plaintiffs' expert, Mtre.
Letendre, when he observes that: "
After all, the Genetic Implication in the Sacks family
was independent of Corey's condition
"
[33]
.

[
97
]

Dr. Watters had specific, important, conclusive
knowledge of a grave danger looming over that family.  Moreover, an important
part of this knowledge was based on research made possible thanks to Edythe's
written permission
[34]
.  Having consented to the research, Edythe was, in a very real
sense, already in the loop.

[
98
]

What obstacle of any sort - professional,
ethical, moral, physical or otherwise - stood in the way of Dr. Watters'
advising Edythe and Beverly directly about the genetic implications arising
from the Uncles' condition?
[35]
There was no need to breach the confidentiality of the Carins in
doing so.  All he had to do was refer to the Uncles and perhaps the Article.
If Edythe or Beverly wanted to know if he had any other information, he could
then refuse to say more on the grounds of confidentiality.  They might not have
been satisfied, but they would have been warned.

[
99
]

Dr. Watters had no ethical obstacle to warning
Edythe and Beverly of the genetic implications.  More critically, he had the
obligation to do so.  His omission in that regard is a fault under the general
rules of civil liability.

G.2     The failure to request permission from Frank

[
100
]

Accepting strictly for the sake of argument defence counsel's
hypothesis that the obligation of confidentiality restricted Dr. Watters'
options, the question still arises as to why he did not simply ask Frank's
permission to communicate the genetic implications to the Sacks Family
directly.  Given the roadblock of unknown duration concerning Audrey's
emotional state, coupled with what he considered to be Frank's good faith and
cooperation, he could have assumed that he would be granted that permission.

[
101
]

Moreover, time was of the essence.

[
102
]

As of May 31, 1971 when Dr. Fitch first intervened, Dr. Watters was
aware of the Uncles' condition.  Shortly thereafter, as seen from the family
tree appearing in the 1973 Article, he also became aware that Edythe had an
adult daughter.  Beverly's presence underlined the need to move quickly in case
she might become pregnant.  Waiting for an indefinite period until Audrey was
ready to deal with the matter was not an acceptable option.

[
103
]

Dr. Watters was in contact with Frank until 1974, when he did
additional testing on Corey.  It would have taken little effort to request his
permission to communicate with Edythe and Beverly, assuming he needed that.
Moreover, his own expert, Dr. Rosenblatt, testified that he would have expected
Dr. Watters to ask Frank by then whether he had discussed the matter with
Audrey or, at the very minimum, what was the situation
with his wife
[36]
.  Passivity was not appropriate in the circumstances.

[
104
]

In light of his obligation to inform Edythe and Beverly, as
described above, his omission to seek Frank's approval to do that is a fault
under the general rules of civil liability.

G.3     The failure to follow through concerning
Audrey

[
105
]

A third fault lies in Dr. Watters' omission to persist in ensuring
that Audrey was adequately warned of and counselled on the genetic
implications.  This had implications not only for Audrey's future children, but
also for the Sacks Family, whom, in Defendants' view, Audrey had an obligation
to warn in turn.

[
106
]

There was, of course, no ethical obstacle to his speaking directly
to Audrey.  Instead, defence counsel rely on the practices of doctors in the
early 1970s.  Their experts opined that, according to the practice at that
time, it was sufficient to advise either parent verbally of the genetic
implications, as was done in the July 1971 telephone call to Frank.

[
107
]

Whether such a level of notice might suffice in general theory is
irrelevant.  It does not respond to the hard fact of Dr. Watters' being told
that, at least for the time being, the critical information would not be passed
on.  At the end of that telephone conversation, it would have been clear to any
reasonable person that important steps remained to be taken, and that there was
no firm plan in place as to how or when to take them.  The issue was far from
closed.

[
108
]

Dr. Fitch's presence is, once again, a complicating factor that
undoubtedly had the effect of misleading Dr. Watters.  Another element that
would have thrown him off was the seemingly unconscionable behaviour of Frank.

[
109
]

As for Frank's actions, Audrey states that he said nothing to her
about what he learned from his conversations with Dr. Watters in June and July
1971 or about the need to warn others of the genetic implications.  Although a
pharmacist and an educated man, Frank apparently had serious personal problems,
including drug abuse and a violent streak that required Audrey to seek medical
treatment for herself on New Year's Eve 1971.  The break-up of the couple
shortly after that would not have been conducive to harmonious future
relations.

[
110
]

The Court is convinced that Frank did not do what common sense and
human decency required him to do in this matter.  This is supported by the fact
that, had he been even mildly concerned for Audrey and the Sacks Family, he
would almost certainly have sought further contact with Dr. Watters or, at the
very least, spoken to him about the issue when they met in 1974.

[
111
]

Dr. Watters testified that Frank said nothing about it then and the
Court believes him.  This convinces us of Frank's egregious omission.

[
112
]

It also should have been a red light for Dr. Watters, particularly
since, by that time, he knew the couple had broken up.  In spite of all this,
Dr. Watters never took the next essential step.

[
113
]

As for Dr. Fitch, given her personal contact with Frank, as well as
her intimate knowledge of the history of Audrey's family, it must have seemed
obvious that she would be providing genetic counselling to both him and Audrey
concerning the genetic implications of Corey's illness.  But here again, in
light of the drastic consequences at play, it was necessary to dot every
"i" and cross every "t".  Dr. Watters did not follow
through with Dr. Fitch on the question, a fact that seems almost
incomprehensible given their work together on an article dealing with this very
problem.

[
114
]

In light of the obligation to inform imposed on him, his omission to
ensure that Audrey was fully informed in this regard is a fault under the
general rules of civil liability.

H.      DR. FITCH'S involvement

[
115
]

Dr. Fitch's role remains something of a mystery, even after two
weeks of trial.  Having passed away, she did not testify before us, nor was she
examined on discovery.  Dr. Watters was the only witness before the Court who
admitted having some knowledge of her activities in relation to the matters at
hand, but they were not regular collaborators, not working out of the same
hospital.

[
116
]

Dr. Fitch had a Ph.D. from Columbia University in Genetics and an
M.D. from McGill University.  On September 3, 1968, she began working as a
Staff Investigator in the Lady Davis Institute for Medical Research of the
Jewish General (the "
Lady Davis
") and a Research Associate in
the Department of Pediatrics
(Exhibit
DJGH-2)
.

[
117
]

We have already laid out most of the facts relevant to her
involvement.  It would have been useful had the evidence provided more, since
several important questions remain unanswered.  Not the least of those
questions is how Dr. Fitch came to know about the Uncles and, subsequently,
what contact she had with members of Edythe's family in relation to her work on
the Article.

[
118
]

Audrey testified that Frank did not know about her two cousins (the
Uncles), so it doesn't seem likely that Dr. Fitch learned of them from him.  As
well, it appears that Dr. Fitch had not yet obtained access to the Uncles'
medical records from the Royal Vic when she accompanied Frank on May 31, 1971.
Only after that meeting did she and Dr. Watters discuss the need to get those.

[
119
]

On the other hand, she obviously had knowledge of Edythe and her
family by then.  Edythe eventually signed an authorization form allowing her
access the Uncles' Royal Vic records (the "
Royal Vic Authorization
":

Exhibit DJGH-4
).  Nevertheless, Edythe states that she never met her and, as we
note below, the form is equivocal as to whether Dr. Fitch had personally spoken
with Edythe about the document.

[
120
]

The most likely source of her knowledge is Dr. Cohen.  Both he and
Dr. Fitch worked at the Jewish General, as did Audrey before Corey's birth.
After the birth, Audrey returned to work but states that she does not recall
any conversations about Corey with anyone there.  However, Dr. Cohen, her
former boss and Corey's treating physician, might well have known about the
Uncles.

[
121
]

It is unlikely that this mystery will ever be solved, but that is
not a serious impediment to the Court's analysis in the present case.  It is a
link missing from a chain other than the one binding us here.

I.       DR. FITCH'S FAULT

[
122
]

The Court finds that the radius of contact between Dr. Fitch and
Edythe was such that, given the gravity of the genetic implications, an
obligation to inform was imposed on Dr. Fitch with respect to Edythe and her
family
[37]
.

[
123
]

The contact here was even tighter than in Dr. Watters' case.  Whether
or not there existed a doctor-patient relationship as such, Dr. Fitch was in
communication either directly or indirectly with Edythe concerning the medical
situation of the Uncles.  Although the Royal Vic Authorization could suggest
that Dr. Fitch was not physically present when Edythe signed it
[38]
, it is nevertheless obvious that there was some form of
communication between them, perhaps through a third person.

[
124
]

That is enough in these circumstances.

[
125
]

As a result, the Court will proceed to consider whether there were
any professional or ethical obstacles to Dr. Fitch's advising the Sacks Family
of the genetic implications and whether she committed a fault in not warning
them.

[
126
]

As for ethical obstacles, the Court sees no obligation of
confidentiality that would exclude Edythe and her family from being advised of
the results of Dr. Fitch's research.  We come to this conclusion in spite of
two opinions from eminent experts attempting to show the opposite.

[
127
]

Dr. Claude Laberge starts his report by pointing out that in the
early 1970s there existed no specific norms concerning the communication to
research subjects of the information obtained in the course of research
projects.  He then explains what the practice was at the time.

[
128
]

At pages 3 and 4 of his opinion
(Exhibit DJGH-6)
, Dr. Laberge
states:

Selon la pratique qui prévalait à l'époque
dans un contexte d'études de cas sur dossier, les médecins chercheurs n'avaient
pas l'habitude de communiquer directement avec les personnes … dont les
dossiers avaient été étudiés pour les informer de leurs conclusions.

Tout ce que le médecin chercheur pouvait
décider à l'époque … était de s'assurer que le médecin traitant … connaisse les
conclusions de la recherche.  Il revenait alors au médecin traitant de décider
de l'opportunité de transmettre ces conclusions à son patient … avec les
explications et recommandations nécessaires.

…

Quant aux … membres de la famille élargie,
… il n'était pas de pratique habituelle que le médecin traitant du sujet index
(the patient) les contacte pour les informer directement des conclusions de la
recherche.

…

Compte tenu de la pratique et des normes de
la recherche en vigueur à cette époque, le seul souci qu'aurait pu avoir Dr
Fitch était de s'assurer que le médecin traitant de Corey Carin … connaisse les
hypothèses de transmission héréditaire découlant de l'étude familiale, ce qui a
évidemment été fait parce que le médecin traitant, Dr. Watters, était l'auteur
principal (of the Article).

…

Dans ces circonstances, et à la lumière des pratiques généralement
reconnues à l'époque, Dr Fitch n'avait pas à contacter les membres de la (Sacks
Family) pour les informer des conclusions (of the Article) et leur prodiguer
quelque conseil génétique que ce soit"
.

[
129
]

The Court notes that he does not say that she was under any
obligation
not
to inform the Sacks Family of the genetic implications.
True, the second paragraph cited above seems to indicate that she could not do
more than ensure that the treating physician was aware of the results, but in
light of his other statements, the Court does not read this sentence as a
limitation on the researcher's range of possible actions.  His principal
message is that the usual practice among researchers was not to communicate
with either the research subjects or their extended families.

[
130
]

In any case, Dr. Laberge's opinion is of limited value for several
reasons.

[
131
]

Dr. Laberge was unaware both of the contact between Dr. Fitch and
Edythe and of Dr. Fitch's very direct involvement with at least Frank.  This
information is critical; it moves the case well outside of the limits of a
typical research project.

[
132
]

As a result, he was not in a position to opine on the real question
before us, i.e., what Dr. Fitch could or couldn't - or should or shouldn't -
have done in the particular circumstances of this case.

[
133
]

Another aspect that weakens his opinion arose in cross-examination.
It took laborious questioning to corner him into admitting that Dr. Watters
erred in presuming that Dr. Fitch would tell the Sacks family of the genetic
implications, thus freeing him from any obligation to do so.  The other experts
answered with no apparent hesitation, even though their answers were
unfavourable to Dr. Watters.

[
134
]

This behaviour forces the Court to conclude that Dr. Laberge lacked
objectivity in his opinion and testimony.  In that light, his opinions are less
convincing than what we would have preferred.

[
135
]

Professor Bartha Knoppers also provided an opinion for the
hospital.  Its scope is limited to the following.

a.  On the
subject of "
Ethical Norms
Governing Research (1966-1974)
", she quotes the
Canadian Medical Association's 1970
Code of Ethics
to the effect that
physicians should protect the patient's secrets, to conclude that "
Dr. Fitch was only obliged to secrecy
regarding the medical records and not to a duty of disclosure".

b.  On the
subject of "
Professional
Norms Governing Physicians
", basing herself on the

Quebec Medical Act
of 1973, she notes that research was not considered a
medical act in 1973.  As a result, Dr. Fitch was not involved in any

that "
the fact she wasn't
the physician of Edythe Sacks or Beverly Sacks renders a duty to disclose
inexistent
".

c.  Finally, on
the subject of "
Norms
Governing Access by Researchers to Medical Records"
, her opinion is that "
having access to medical records of patients in a

de novo

duty of disclosure, since there was no professional relationship between Dr.
Fitch and Beverly and Edythe Sacks
".

[
136
]

Here again, the focus is misdirected in light of the specific facts
of this case.

[
137
]

Even under the premise that a duty of confidentiality is relevant,
she does not say that Dr. Fitch was under an obligation
not
to inform
the Sacks Family of the genetic implications.  Moreover, among the medical

could the obligation of confidentiality create an impediment to her
communicating with the Uncles' mother?

[
138
]

As for the duty to inform, she had to limit her analysis to the area
of her professional expertise: professional and ethical norms in the medical
field.  She quite properly left to the Court the appreciation of a general
obligation under the law.

[
139
]

In any event, the only medical-ethical question that might have some
relevance was answered definitively by Dr. Norman Kalant, the Director of
Research at the Lady Davis at the time of the Article.  Testifying as an
ordinary witness, as opposed to an expert, he replied without hesitation to the

the subjects of research the results of their investigations: "
No.  I don't believe that there was
anything preventing them
"
[39]
.

[
140
]

In light of the above, the Court concludes that no professional or
ethical obstacle impeded Dr. Fitch's advising the Sacks Family of the genetic
implications.

[
141
]

That settled, the question of whether or not she committed a fault
in not warning them has already been answered in light of her duty to inform.
Our analysis of Dr. Watters' first fault applies here, as well.  Dr. Fitch
therefore committed the same type of fault as he did by omitting to communicate
directly with Edythe and Beverly.

J.       THE JEWISH GENERAL'S
INVOLVEMENT

[
142
]

Generally, and in spite of
article 1463
of the
Civil Code
[40]
, a hospital is not responsible for the work of the doctors
practicing there.  This applies equally to doctors who are employees of the
hospital doing independent research.  This is because there exists no supervisory
authority of the employer hospital over their work.

[
143
]

Dr. Norman Kalant testified on the independence of researchers at
the Lady Davis in the early 1970s.  Based on his testimony, the Court is
satisfied that, as a general rule, there was no supervisory authority exercised
by the Jewish General over those researchers at the relevant time.  In the case
of Dr. Fitch, however, two exhibits and Dr. Kalant's further testimony require
the Court to look deeper into the issue
[41]
.

[
144
]

Concerning the first of those exhibits, P-17, at the time of Dr.
Fitch's hiring, Dr. Leonard Pinsky, "
Director, Division Medical Genetics
", wrote the following in a July 1968 letter to Dr. Michael
Gold, with a copy to Dr. Kalant:

under my
supervision
.  Her clinical areas of responsibility will include sex
chromatin determination, dermatoglyphics
and genetic counselling
.  Her
research will deal with those patients (and their families) whose problems
merit further investigation and eventual publication.  I am confident that she

Although
she has no real experience in this area, her background will enable her to

.

Director, Division Medical Genetics

Copy:  Dr. Norman Kalant

(The Court's underlining)

[
145
]

The second exhibit is the Royal Vic Authorization.  Presumably
shortly after Dr. Watters agreed in 1971 to collaborate on the Article and Dr.

undated document.  We reproduce its text below, the bold portions showing text
that was printed or typed and the italicized portions showing text written by
hand:

I hereby authorize the

Royal Victoria

Hospital, to allow: Dr. N. Fitch
and Dr.
L. Pinsky
, to study the medical chart
(s)

of:

(1)
unamed
(sic)
child born on […], 1941   (2) Michael –
born on […] 1946

Jack Sacks

(Signature)

Please fill in both birth dates

(The Court's underlining)

[
146
]

Counsel for the hospital attempted to explain away the relevance of the
pairing of the researchers in the Royal Vic Authorization by asserting, and it
seems to be so, that the document is a pre-prepared form (i.e., the text in
bold above) with blanks to be filled in by hand for the information relevant to
a particular project.  As such, it should not be taken as a conscious, on-going
decision to pair the doctors for supervisory purposes.

[
147
]

That might be one way to see it, but it can also indicate that the
hospital was wilfully and consistently pairing Dr. Fitch with Dr. Pinsky for
research purposes even three years after her hiring.  When read with Exhibit
P-17, it also indicates that that pairing was in order for Dr. Pinsky to
supervise her work
[42]
.

[
148
]

Dr. Kalant testified on Exhibit P-17, subject to an objection by
Plaintiffs that he is not a proper witness, being neither the author nor the
recipient of this letter.  The Court took the objection under reserve and will
rule on it now.

[
149
]

Dr. Kalant was copied on the letter and its contents fell within his
jurisdiction as Director of Research at the Lady Davis.  Moreover, Plaintiffs'
counsel had previously questioned him on it, at which time he stated that he
had seen it before.  The Court is thus satisfied that he is a proper witness
for questions relating to the exhibit and, accordingly, dismisses the
objection.

[
150
]

His testimony is enlightening.  To the question why he would have
been copied on the letter, he replied: "
I presume because Dr. Pinsky wanted me to know how he
felt about this arrangement
"
[43]
.  The word "arrangement" is his.

[
151
]

To the next question: "
And do you know if there was any importance for you to
know what the terms of the arrangement were?
", he
replied:

Well,
I knew what the arrangement was that we had in place for every other
investigator, and that is that once employed, they were to be...they were to
function as independent investigators.  If they still needed supervision, as
this letter appears to indicate, then we would not have hired such person.  It
was contrary to what the principle of independence means.

[
152
]

Dr. Kalant says that the Pinsky letter appears to indicate that Dr.
Fitch needed supervision.  It certainly does that, particularly given the
phrase: "
Although she has
no real experience in this area
", in the last
sentence.  This testimony, read in the light of exhibits P-17 and the Royal Vic
Authorization, raises the possibility that the "arrangement" for Dr.
Fitch might not have been the same one in place for "
every other investigator
".  But he goes on to say that, in those circumstances, the
Lady Davis would not have hired her as an independent investigator.

[
153
]

What, then, is one to make of the point that she was, in fact,
hired?

[
154
]

One must remember that she started at the Lady Davis some three
years before she began work on the Article.  Although the proof shows that some
supervision of her work might have been initially exercised, it flows from Dr.
Kalant's testimony that this would not have been tolerated for long.

[
155
]

It is particularly revealing that Dr. Watters never mentions Dr.
Pinsky.  Although it does not appear that he was ever asked the question
directly, it seems logical that he would have talked about him had he played
any sort of role, particularly if Dr. Fitch was in any way reporting to him.

[
156
]

Other than his name on the Royal Vic Authorization, there is nothing
in the evidence to indicate that Dr. Pinsky was involved with Dr. Fitch's work
on the Article.  That form is not enough to establish the principal-agent
relationship required for the hospital's liability.  This lack of evidence,
reinforced by Dr. Watters' silence on the point, leads us to find that
Plaintiffs have not met their burden of proof on this issue.

[
157
]

For these reasons, the Court concludes that
article 1463
does not
apply and that the Jewish General is not liable for the damages caused by the
fault of Dr. Fitch.

K.       causation

[
158
]

A finding of fault against a party is not sufficient to hold it
civilly liable for damages suffered by a plaintiff.
Article 1607
of the
Civil
Code
requires that those damages be an "
immediate and direct
"
consequence of that fault.  In an impressive review of the law on medical
liability, our colleague, Michel Delorme, J.S.C., put it this way: "
But for that fault, would Plaintiff have
sustained the damages that he is claiming?
"
[44]

[
159
]

Causality is a question of fact and, as in all such questions, it
must be established on a basis of probability: "
Evidence is sufficient if it renders the existence of
a fact more probable than its non existence, unless the law requires more
convincing proof
"
(Art. 2804 C.C.Q.)
.  The
Supreme Court noted in
Laferrière v. Lawson
that "
Causation in law must be established on the
balance of probabilities, taking into account all the evidence: factual,
statistical and that which the judge is entitled to presume. … If after
consideration of these factors a judge is not satisfied that the fault has, on
his or her assessment of the balance of probabilities, caused any real damage,
then the recovery should be denied
".
[45]

[
160
]

The Defendants assert that a link is missing in the chain of
causality in this case.  Even had a fault been committed by either doctor,
which they deny, and damages suffered, which they admit, they contend that
there is either no, or insufficient, proof that it is probable that such fault
is the immediate and direct cause of those damages.

[
161
]

The Defendants submit that one must ask what would have happened, on
a balance of probabilities, had Edythe been warned.  Is it probable that she
would have warned Beverly and/or Marcy and, furthermore, that Marcy would have
taken the necessary steps to avoid giving birth to Jacob?  The burden of proof
rests with Marcy on this point.

[
162
]

In Audrey's case, they submit that she has the burden of showing
that, had Dr. Watters warned her of the genetic implications, it is probable
that she would have acted likewise with respect to Yochai's birth.

[
163
]

Defendants caution that, in these families, this is not as obvious
as one might expect.  They contend that the proof shows a reticence to discuss
this type of matter openly and frankly even between sisters, much less between
a niece and an aunt or between cousins.  They say that this would be
particularly so where that niece/cousin moved thousands of kilometres away to
Israel in 1977 and only visited Canada infrequently since then.

[
164
]

Plaintiffs' proof is complicated by the fact that, given the time
elapsed from the date of the alleged faults, several key persons were
unavailable to testify at trial.  Among the missing were Frank, Nathalie and
Edythe, although the latter was examined on discovery by the opposing party and
the transcript was filed.

[
165
]

That examination does not shed much light on Edythe's openness to
share the type of information in question with her own daughter or
granddaughter.  It does show that she did not discuss either Corey's or
Yochai's situation in detail or at length with Nathalie or Audrey.  Her
explanation seems reasonable: "
Wouldn't it be hurting her (Audrey) to have her repeat when you could
see that there was something wrong?
".
[46]

[
166
]

But why stop at Edythe?  Beverly would have been an active participant
in this process.  She testified and corroborated Edythe's version that there
was little discussion or knowledge of Corey's or Yochai's situation within the
Sacks Family.  She stated that all she was told about Corey was that he had
brain problems and, as for Yochai, that he had trouble breathing.  Upon
returning from a visit to Israel, Nathalie told her that Yochai was "
not well
", but
gave no details.

[
167
]

Defendants' counsel submit that, given the absence of clear evidence
on the point, the only way to supply the missing link in the causality chain is
by way of a presumption of fact to be drawn from the proof presented.  They
maintain that, based on the testimony of Edythe and Beverly, it is not possible
to make the presumption that, had they been warned, one of them would have
alerted Marcy to the illness that runs in their family and to the genetic
implications thereof.

[
168
]

As for Audrey's likely decision to give birth to Yochai, Defendants
also insist that it is necessary to make a presumption of fact in order to
establish causality.  As in the other case, they argue that no such presumption
is possible.

L.       PRESUMPTIONS OF FACT

[
169
]

A presumption is defined as "
an inference established by law or the court from a
known fact to an unknown fact
"
(Art. 2846 C.C.Q.)
.
As well, although presumptions are left to the discretion of the Court, article
2849 requires it to take "
only
serious, precise and concordant presumptions into consideration
".

[
170
]

Is it possible for the Court to make such a presumption concerning
the causal link in these files?

[
171
]

In the case of the Trossmans, the Court has no hesitation in doing
so.  Audrey's case is different.

[
172
]

Concerning the Trossmans, Beverly testified that she had a good
relationship with her mother and that they were, and still are, very close.
She added that the same is true of her relationship with her daughter, and
Marcy's testimony corroborated this.

[
173
]

As well, the issue in question is not a minor point of family
gossip.  It is life or death information - in a sense, even more critical than
life or death.  These women are carriers of a horrendous genetic disease.
There are those who would say that death is mild in comparison, for then only
one life is lost.  With PMD, every one in the family is condemned in a very
real way.

[
174
]

The Court finds that it is, therefore, probable that Edythe or
Beverly would have warned Marcy.  It is simply unimaginable that at least one
of them would not have done so.  To borrow Audrey's word, it would take a
"monster" not to warn one's family of such a thing.  Frank's sin
would seem mild in comparison.

[
175
]

Defendants' counsel seem to assume that the genetic implication
flowing from the Uncles' connection to Corey would have been given only to
Edythe and that it would have been left up to her to communicate the information
to Beverly and, eventually, Marcy.  That does not stand to reason.

[
176
]

No reasonable person in 1971, knowing the existence of Beverly and
perhaps Marcy, would have limited his efforts to informing only Edythe.  He
would surely have communicated the genetic implications to all members of the
Sacks Family that needed to know, and Beverly, being of childbearing age,
certainly needed to know - even more than Edythe!

[
177
]

As well, the information session would not have been a short,
informal conversation.  Genetic counselling would have had to take place and no
genetic counsellor would have ignored two live potential carriers of the
disease.

[
178
]

Beverly testified that, had she known the genetic implications, she
would have told Marcy when she was old enough and sought professional help.
What intelligent, rational parent would not do the same?

[
179
]

As for the likelihood that Marcy and Andrew would have taken the
proper steps if they had knowledge of the genetic implications, there can be no
doubt.  After Jacob's birth, they became obsessed in finding a diagnosis for
him.  Once the diagnosis was discovered, they searched around the world for
doctors who might be able to help him.  They canvassed pharmaceutical companies
to see if there might be an experimental drug that could be of some use.  Marcy
wrote articles about their experiences and created a Website.  They even
started a foundation to aid in PMD research.

[
180
]

Later, she terminated one male pregnancy after testing positive and
underwent
in vitro
fertilization in order to give birth to healthy twin
girls, first having the embryos tested in order to be sure that they would be
free of PMD.

[
181
]

Marcy and Andrew are highly educated, inquisitive and determined and
they would have understood the genetic implications, even if they had not yet
experienced them.  It is inconceivable that they would not have done as Marcy
testified, i.e., tested for the illness and terminated the pregnancy.  By 2002,

in utero
testing for PMD was available, as was therapeutic abortion.

[
182
]

The Court therefore makes whatever presumptions of fact are
necessary in order to hold that the faults of Drs. Watters and Fitch were the
legal cause of the damages suffered by the Trossmans.

[
183
]

As we stated above, Audrey's case is different.

[
184
]

Her behaviour with regards to Corey and his condition was not what
one would normally expect.  Although she appears to have conducted herself as a
responsible, mature and loving adult and mother towards Yochai, the proof
indicates that this was not the case after Corey's birth.

[
185
]

It is not the Court's purpose or desire to judge her for how she
reacted to Corey's situation.  The shock and disappointment that his condition
must have created in her is only human and only she knows what tumult was
raging in her head and heart in that regard.

[
186
]

What the Court must judge, however, is whether it should presume
that, had she received further information on the genetic implications attached
to Corey's illness, she would have avoided giving birth to Yochai
[47]
.  The Court speaks of "further information" because it
finds as a fact that in May 1970 Dr. Watters did provide what we would qualify
as "preliminary and conditional" information to her.

[
187
]

The Court must also keep in mind that Audrey has the burden of proof
on this question.

[
188
]

To make such a presumption, the Court must find that it is
"serious, precise and concordant"
, in the words of article 2849.  The Court of Appeal, through the
pen of Antonio Lamer, J.C.A. (as he then was), defined these terms as follows:

Presumptions are serious when the connection between the known fact and
the unknown fact is such that the existence of one establishes the existence of
the other in a clear and obvious manner.

Presumptions are precise when the conclusions that flow from the known
fact tend to establish the contested unknown fact in a direct and specific
manner.

Finally, they are concordant, whether or not they each spring from a
common or different source, when they tend to establish the fact to be proven
through their overall relationship and consistency.
[48]
(translation)

[
189
]

Professor Royer is of the view that a presumption cannot be drawn
where the known facts can reasonably lead to a conclusion incompatible with the
unknown fact that a party is trying to prove, or where they do not reasonably
allow one to exclude other causes
[49]
.  Although this
follows from the burden of proof being on the party evoking the presumption,
the Court would still consider deciding in favour of the "unknown
fact" where it is clearly the most likely conclusion that can be drawn,
even though other conclusions could not be excluded.

[
190
]

But such theoretical cogitations are not necessary in this case.  It
is possible to arrive at more than one conclusion as to Audrey's likely
response after receiving further information, several of which are incompatible
with an outcome favourable to Audrey and none of which are clearly more likely
than the others.

[
191
]

After the meeting with Dr. Watters on May 12, 1970, Audrey should
have been concerned about having other children with the same syndrome.
Nevertheless, she appears to have completely erased this
caveat
from her
mind.

[
192
]

The fact that she had four more children in Israel without
requesting specific testing, or even mentioning Corey's problems to her doctors
there certainly supports that view
[50]
.  It is also consistent
with Frank's statements in June 1971 that she was not able to handle
information about the diagnosis and the genetic implications.

[
193
]

She testified that in the period after Corey's birth it was too
difficult for her to see him.  Although she at first stated that she phoned
Ambar at least once a week for news, she later implied that she got most of her
information through telephone conversations with her ex in-laws.  It is not
clear how often those calls occurred or when they stopped, but it seems obvious
that all communication about Corey ceased by the time she moved to Israel in
1977, even though Corey lived until 1983.

[
194
]

Even after Yochai's birth she seemed to be in denial.  "
I made no connection between Yochai and
Corey.  It never even dawned on me
", she
testified.  She only admits becoming aware of a genetic disorder in her family
when Marcy e-mailed her in 2003 about the discoveries she and Andrew had made
concerning PMD.

[
195
]

One of several conclusions that flow from this evidence is that
Audrey was unable to deal with the reality of Corey's condition and preferred,
or needed, to insulate herself from it.  This leads to the conclusion that,
even had Dr. Watters communicated further with her, she would not have been
receptive to his message.  We recognize that the opposite conclusion is also
possible, but is not so obvious as to allow us to presume one way or the
other.

[
196
]

Given the onus on Audrey, this ambivalence in the proof is fatal to
the causal link between Dr. Watters' fault towards her and the moral damages
she alleges.  It is also, therefore, fatal to her claim
[51]
.

M.      AUDREY LISS AS DEFENDANT IN
WARRANTY

[
197
]

Dr. Watters calls Audrey in warranty for failing to warn the Sacks
Family of the genetic implications.  His allegations set out his position
clearly:

20.   Defendant in Warranty, Mrs. Audrey Liss, also had the
opportunity and a duty to inform her immediate family, whom she was meeting on
a regular basis, of the nature of her sons’ condition and the very distinct
possibility that their condition was one in which familial incidence had been
frequently observed.

21.   Plaintiff in Warranty declares that Defendant in
Warranty, Audrey Liss, was aware of the similarity between the condition of her
son Corey and her other son Yockai (sic) Liss and that this condition had
genetic characteristics and could be transmitted to a male offspring in her
maternal line.

22.

Plaintiff in
Warranty declares that Defendant in Warranty, Audrey Liss, had a moral and
familial duty to advise her immediate family in her maternal side, of the
possibility that any male child born to a female representative of that line,
could suffer from the same condition and that in fact, Defendant in Warranty,
Audrey Liss, was aware of this connection and of this possibility when the
diagnosis on her younger son was made and confirmed in her new country
residence Israel.

23.   Plaintiff in Warranty declares that Defendant in
Warranty, Audrey Liss, was in contact with her family in Montreal and that her
mother and her maternal aunt, Mrs. Sacks, grandmother of Marcy White, had
numerous family and social contacts between them and that Ms. Audrey Liss,
herself, visited her family in Canada on several occasions in the 10 years that
preceded the birth of Jacob Trossman.

24.   Plaintiff in Warranty declares that he was, for his
part, never in contact with the Sacks or the White families, did not know them
in any way and was not in a position to contact them even after having advised
Mr. Franklin Carin of his diagnosis in 1971 and thereafter.

25.   Defendant in Warranty, Mrs. Audry Liss, is therefore
herself responsible for not having advised her immediate family of this serious
possibility, allowing them to eventually take the necessary precautions
concerning future conceptions particularly in view of the fact well-known in
their family that two of Mrs. Marcy White’s uncles had exhibited similar
symptoms one generation before.

[
198
]

In his oral pleadings, Dr. Watters' attorney specified that Audrey's
conduct should be treated as a
novus actus interveniens
[52]
or, at the very least, a contributory fault.

[
199
]

As a preliminary remark, we underline the need to keep in mind our
finding of fact that Frank never told Audrey of Corey's final diagnosis or of
the genetic implications flowing from it and that Audrey's mind was, in any
event, closed, or at least confused, on the subject.  As such, her
understanding of Corey's condition was limited to Dr. Watters' comments in the
one, pre-diagnosis meeting at a time when she was having great trouble dealing
with the issue.

[
200
]

In the Action in Warranty, the Court will
consider:

a.  whether Audrey knew or should have known that she was a carrier
of an SLD before Jacob's birth;

b.  assuming she did not, whether she committed a fault by not
taking the necessary steps to determine that;

c.  assuming the answer to one of the above questions is
affirmative, whether she committed a fault by not warning the Sacks Family
before Jacob's birth that she was or might be a carrier of an SLD.

[
201
]

In order to succeed in the Action in Warranty, Dr. Watters must
prove either "a" or "b", plus "c".

[
202
]

Two other findings in this judgment must be considered in this
context, that on causation and that on prescription.

[
203
]

In the first, we hold that Audrey was unable to deal with the
reality of Corey's condition and preferred, or needed, to insulate herself from
it.  This, however, does not mean that Audrey knew or should have known that
she was the carrier of an SLD before Jacob's birth.  In fact, it points in the
opposite direction.  As we discuss below, vital information was kept from her
by Frank and Dr. Watters.

[
204
]

Regarding prescription, in the next section of this judgment the
Court holds that her recourse against Dr. Watters is prescribed because, at
least by 1997, a reasonably prudent and informed person could have suspected
that a fault had occurred in 1971.  Nevertheless, it does not automatically
follow that she knew or should have known that she was the carrier of an SLD
before Jacob's birth.

[
205
]

As we explain below, the test on prescription is purely objective:
what would a reasonably prudent and informed person suspect in the same
circumstances.  To hold, as we do below, that it was not impossible for her to
act as of 1997 does not mean that she knew what the problem was and appreciated
the impact of the genetic implications.  It does not equate to a fault.

[
206
]

Audrey testified that she first became aware of a genetic disorder
in her family from Marcy's 2003 e-mail.  Opposing counsel assert that she must
have made the association at the time of Yochai's birth, whereas Audrey states
that the association between the conditions of Corey and Yochai "
never even dawned
'
on her.

[
207
]

Genetics is a most sophisticated science, coming of age only within
the last few decades.  There is nothing in the proof to demonstrate that Audrey
