had any understanding of genetics or genetic disorders before 2003, or reason
to suspect she was afflicted with one.  A
"severe congenital neurological disorder"

(Exhibit GWD-1)
is not necessarily hereditary, as we discuss below.

[
208
]

No one had ever spoken to her about a possible connection between
Corey's state and that of the Uncles.  She testified that she thought it was
"
brain damage
", which seems to be the way people referred to such things at
the time.  Also, no diagnosis of Corey before 2003 ever indicated a genetic
problem.  Neither Frank nor Dr. Watters informed her of either of those
critical points.  The one preliminary conversation with Dr. Watters in 1970, at
a time in her life when she was in a fragile emotional state, was certainly not
enough to overcome the gaps in her scientific and factual knowledge or to
educate her to any useful degree on genetic issues.

[
209
]

The proof of her ignorance of the danger lies in the fact that she
sought no genetic testing or counselling during her subsequent pregnancies.
Corey's condition shocked and incapacitated her.  It is inconceivable that, had
she suspected that she was at risk to give birth to a second Corey, she would
have rolled the dice four more times.

[
210
]

Yochai's condition could have opened her eyes, but the proof does
not show that it did.  Although he appears to have had excellent medical care,
he and Audrey lived on an agricultural kibbutz far from urban amenities.  His
condition was never diagnosed before the PMD link was discovered in 2003.  In
addition, she had given birth to three healthy children in between the two sick
boys.  It is thus possible that she did not see a connection between the
problems of this second sick baby and the "
brain damage
" of the
first.

[
211
]

The 1997 Israeli medical report on Yochai
(Exhibit GWD-1)
, which is
pivotal in our finding on prescription, does not play as conclusive a role in
the present context.  That report states that "…
the mother had a son from a previous marriage who
suffered from a severe congenital neurological disorder …
".  Accepting that this shows that Audrey had spoken to her
Israeli doctors about Corey by then, it does not demonstrate that she – or even
they - suspected that there was a hereditary aspect to Yochai's illness.
Nothing in the evidence suggests it and, more vividly, those doctors did not
cause Audrey's other three children, teenagers at the time, to be tested or
counselled for possible genetic problems.

[
212
]

In light of her not having been informed of critical facts, and
considering the burden of proof that applies, the Court is of the view that
Defendant has not proven that Audrey knew or should have known that she was the
carrier of an SLD before Jacob's birth.

[
213
]

Our analysis on the first question essentially answers the second,
as well.  Given her lack of knowledge and understanding of the matter, she
cannot have been expected to take steps to determine if she was a carrier of an
SLD.

[
214
]

As a result of the absence of fault on these questions, the third
must be answered in the negative.  She cannot have committed a fault in not
advising the Sacks Family before Jacob's birth that she might be a carrier of
an SLD, since she was unaware of that through no fault of her own.

[
215
]

Consequently, since we find that she committed no fault, there can
be no
novus actus interveniens
or contributory fault attributable to
her.

[
216
]

The Action in Warranty is therefore dismissed, but without costs.
There are a number of reasons for refusing costs at this level, a decision that
we shall also apply to her in the principal action, although there, in her favour.

[
217
]

In the first place, she did not file a defence to the Action in
Warranty.  Her financial exposure for professional fees and disbursements would
therefore be minimal.  In any event, any expert's fees will be covered by the
order in favour of the Trossmans.

[
218
]

Another factor is that her testimony in discovery, and later at
trial, was uncooperative.  Her pat answer to too many questions was "I
don't recall", and the Court felt that she was not making a sincere effort
to respond adequately.  This forced the Court to intervene in order to request
her to put her mind to the issues and give as much
information as she could.  Unfortunately, things did not improve significantly
after that.  Such conduct deserves sanctioning.

[
219
]

Finally, in the principal action, the Court dismisses her claim
against Dr. Watters both for lack of causation and for prescription.  Normally,
costs would be awarded against her there on the basis of her claim for moral
damages of $150,000.  Given our ruling on costs in the Action in Warranty, it
seems only fair to shield her from those in the principal action.

[
220
]

Thus, the Court will grant costs neither to her in the Action in
Warranty nor against her in the Watters Action.

N.      PRESCRIPTION

[
221
]

Paraphrasing
articles 2875
and
2921
of the
Civil Code
, extinctive
prescription is a means of being released from an obligation by the mere lapse
of time, in that it extinguishes a right that has not been used.  With respect
to claims such as the ones in these files, article 2925 provides that the
period required to prescribe is three years.

[
222
]

In the Watters Action, Dr. Watters contends that Audrey's claim is
prescribed: prescription would have begun to run as of Yochai's birth in 1988
and her action was instituted only on May 5, 2005.

[
223
]

He does not contend that the Trossmans' claim is prescribed.  That
action having been instituted on May 5, 2005, this was within three years of
their discovery of the Article on February 24, 2003
[53]
.  He admits that
this is the date on which prescription would have commenced to run on that
claim.

[
224
]

In the Fitch Action, originally instituted on February 23, 2006, Dr.
Fitch does not raise prescription.  The Jewish General does plead it, however:
prescription would have begun to run on February 25, 2003
[54]
, but the action was amended to include the hospital only on August
20, 2007, some four and one-half years later.

[
225
]

Dealing first with the Watters Action, although we have already
dismissed Audrey's claim for another reason, we shall analyze Dr. Watters'
argument that, in any event, it is prescribed.

[
226
]

He asserts that prescription would have started to run in her case
shortly after Yochai's birth in 1988, since she was then in a position to know,
or at least seriously suspect, that there was a genetic problem in her family
and, therefore, that Dr. Watters might have committed a fault by not warning
her of that seventeen years earlier.

[
227
]

Prescription in matters such as this is based on objective criteria
[55]
, commencing to run from the date when a reasonably prudent and
informed person could suspect a connection between damages he has suffered and
a faulty act
[56]
.  The question here is whether that date in Audrey's case was
before or after May 5, 2002: three years before she sued Dr. Watters.

[
228
]

Yochai was her third son and the second with a similar problem.  The
fathers were different.  Upon seeing Yochai, a reasonably prudent and informed
person would likely have thought of Corey, although Audrey testified that she
did not make the connection
[57]
.

[
229
]

Whatever the case, she appears eventually to have done so.  In
February 1997, a medical report on Yochai
(Exhibit GWD-1)
refers to the
fact that "…
the mother
had a son from a previous marriage who suffered from a severe congenital
neurological disorder …
".  Audrey had obviously
spoken about Corey to her Israeli doctors by then.

[
230
]

This reference would have planted the seed of doubt in the mind of a
reasonably prudent and informed person, assumed it had not already been planted
at the time of Yochai's birth.

[
231
]

Our earlier finding that Audrey was not, in fact, "reasonably
informed" is of no assistance to her.  The test on prescription is an
objective one, based on how the virtual "
bonne mère de famille
"
would act.  Such a person would normally have wondered if there was a link
between the boys' conditions and if Dr. Watters could have known that.

[
232
]

As for the relevance of subjective criteria, the contents of the
report are such that Audrey could no longer allege any "
impossibility in fact to act
" under article 2904 C.C.Q.  She might not have realized at
that time that she had a genetic disorder but, once realizing the
"coincidence" of the two baby boys' conditions, she could no longer
claim it was impossible for her to commence investigations.

[
233
]

The Court thus concludes that, at least by 1997, a reasonably
prudent and informed person could have suspected that Dr. Watters committed a
fault towards her.  This was eight years before she instituted the present
proceedings.

[
234
]

Her action against Dr. Watters is thus prescribed and will be
dismissed.  For reasons already explained, this will be without costs.

[
235
]

Turning to the Fitch Action, no one contends that there was
prescription of the claim against Dr. Fitch.  Since the Trossmans instituted
the original action on February 23, 2006, their claim against her would not
have been prescribed for at least another 24 hours.  As harsh as the rule of
prescription might be with respect to a claim that is even one day late, it is
correspondingly lenient with a claim that is made at the last minute.

[
236
]

The proceedings in the Fitch Action, as amended to add the Jewish
General as defendant, are not clear either as to when the Plaintiffs contend
that prescription began to run or as to why the hospital feels that the action
against it is prescribed.  Each side reproached the other for its lack of clarity
on the point and bemoaned being left guessing until the very end of the trial.

[
237
]

Upon learning on the last day of the trial that the hospital was
contesting the application of
articles 1526
and
2900

C.c.Q.
[58]
, the Trossmans complained of being caught off guard and asked to be
allowed to plead in writing on the point at a later time.  That permission
being granted, a rebuttal right was also accorded to the hospital.

[
238
]

Several weeks later, the Trossmans not only provided notes and
authorities on the point, but also asked to amend their action by adding three
paragraphs, as follows:

17.
THAT
MARCY attempted to
communicate with Dr. FITCH and with Dr. WATTERS shortly after being provided
with a copy of the FITCH ARTICLE on February 24, 2003, but her attempts were
unsuccessful for the following reasons:

a)       The whereabouts of Dr. FITCH were unknown;

b)       Dr. WATTERS did not return MARCY's phone calls despite
messages left by MARCY with the secretary of Dr. WATTERS.

18.
THAT

the
Plaintiffs
did not and could not possibly become aware of the role
of Dr. FITCH and of her relationship with the Jewish General Hospital until the
Examinations on Discovery of Dr. WATTERS in November/December 2005;

19.
THAT

it was accordingly "impossible" (within the meaning of Article 2904 C.C.Q.)
for the Plaintiffs to "act" (i.e. institute legal proceedings)
against the Jewish
General Hospital (and Dr. FITCH)
prior to December 2005;

[
239
]

The Trossmans felt that the amendment might be necessary because of
a statement they cite from the sixth edition of "Baudouin" to the
effect that a party wishing to raise its impossibility to act must specifically
plead the facts relevant to that in its proceedings
[59]
.

[
240
]

The Jewish General contests the amendment on the ground that it is
useless: even assuming that the new facts are true, the claim against it would
still be prescribed and, therefore, the amendment should be refused
[60]
.  The hospital adds that the argument is nothing more than an
afterthought on Plaintiffs' counsel's part, since it was not raised until the
fourth amendment to the action.

[
241
]

The Trossmans counter that, although they now felt that the
statement in Baudouin might not accurately reflect the law, the amendment would
still be useful, particularly at this late stage, in order to bring the
proceedings into line with the proof made at trial.

[
242
]

A hearing was held on the motion to amend some two months after the
conclusion of the trial and the Court decided to rule on it within its judgment
on the merits.  This allowed us to consider the usefulness aspect in light of
our overall evaluation of the facts relevant to prescription.

[
243
]

Considering our ruling on prescription set out below, and the
relevance to that holding of the allegations in the amendment, and considering
that those allegations merely reflect what is already in proof, the Court
grants the motion to amend.

[
244
]

The hospital's argument on prescription is that the original action
against Dr. Fitch did not interrupt prescription against it and, given that,
the amendment came too late.

[
245
]

On the question of interruption, it pleads that
articles 1526
and

2900
of the
Civil Code
do not apply here.  The interruption of prescription
foreseen there occurs only between solidary debtors and not
in solidum

ones.  The facts alleged in the Fitch Action, as amended in August 2007, show
that there could exist only
in solidum
liability between Dr. Fitch and
the Jewish General
[61]
, the latter's liability being not extra-contractual and fault-based
but, rather, statutory and without fault.  Thus, it argues, the original action
did not interrupt prescription against it.

[
246
]

The Court agrees with the hospital's submission on these points
[62]
.  Although under
article 1463
the principal and agent are generally
solidarily liable for the latter's extracontractual fault in the performance of
his duties, that does not necessarily make them solidary debtors.  Where there
is no allegation of fault on the principal's part, as is the case here, that
condition in
article 1526
is not met.  Consequently, they are not solidary
debtors and
article 2900
cannot apply
[63]
.

[
247
]

Nevertheless, we come to the conclusion that the Trossmans' claim
against the hospital was not prescribed prior to the amendment of the Fitch
Action.  Before obtaining information on the relationship between Dr. Fitch and
the Jewish General in late 2005, it was "
impossible in fact for them to act
"
[64]
against the hospital.

[
248
]

Prior to the examinations of Dr. Watters in November and December
2005
[65]
, and to his Amended Defence of November 29, 2005, the only
reference to the Jewish General comes at the beginning of the Article, in
relation to the names of the authors, where one sees the following:

Gordon V. Watters and Naomi Fitch

Departments of
Neurology and Pediatrics, Montreal Children's Hospital, and

Lady Davis Institute for Medical Research,
Jewish General Hospital, Montreal, Canada

[
249
]

In their original actions, the Trossmans sued neither the Children's
nor the Jewish General.  This course of action is proper.  A plaintiff should
not automatically sue the hospital where the doctor's alleged fault occurred,
since there is normally no supervisory authority exercised by the hospital over
a doctor's work.

[
250
]

On this basis, we conclude that the information provided in the
heading of the Article was not enough to cause a reasonable and informed person
to sue either hospital.  To the contrary, in the absence of facts pointing to
an exceptional situation that varies significantly from the normal course of
affairs, one would, and should, assume that there is no liability for the
hospital.  This assumption represents an impossibility to act.  Where an
exceptional situation is found to exist, prescription would commence to run on
the claim against the hospital only upon the discovery of that.

[
251
]

After discovering the Article, the Trossmans tried to follow up with
the doctors.  Marcy attempted to contact both of them upon discovering the
Article.  She could not find a phone number for Dr. Fitch, who had retired
fourteen years earlier in 1989
(Exhibit
DJGH-2),
but was able to find one for Dr. Watters.  She
called him on several occasions and left messages, but he did not return the
calls.  There appears to have been a misunderstanding with his secretary on the
procedure to follow.

[
252
]

The Jewish General faults Marcy for not meeting her burden of
showing that she exercised reasonable diligence in trying to contact Dr. Fitch
in order to verify the relationship between her and the hospital.  It alleges
that she should have explained the specific steps she took in that regard and
that her simple statement that she could not find a phone number for her is not
sufficient to satisfy her burden.

[
253
]

The Court rejects this argument.

[
254
]

What more could she have explained – or done – with respect to
obtaining information about Dr. Fitch?  Her testimony is that she tried to find
her but couldn't, and the proof showing that Dr. Fitch had retired 14 years
earlier certainly corroborates that difficulty.  This is uncontradicted
evidence.  It was up to the hospital to counter by showing that her efforts
were inadequate in the circumstances, but it made no proof in that regard.

[
255
]

The evidence shows that the Trossmans first obtained information of
the relationship between Dr. Fitch and the Jewish General in November 2005,
through both the examination of Dr. Watters and his Amended Defence.  In that examination
of November 3
rd
, at page 80 of the transcript, one sees the
following exchange:

Q:  So let me rephrase that
question, Doctor Watters.  Yourself and, is it Doctor Fitch?  Doctor Fitch …

A:  Yes,
Doctor Fitch, PhD
, yes.
(The Court's underlining)

[
256
]

This is the first indication that Dr. Fitch was other than a medical
doctor, although she was that, too.  It would thus touch a nerve and cause a
reasonably prudent and informed person to wonder if this fact might take the
case outside the typical doctor-hospital relationship.  It would be cause to
investigate the relationship further, whereas everything up to then, including
the heading of the Article, led to believe that this was not necessary.

[
257
]

It is true that the Plaintiffs knew these facts at the time the
Fitch Action was first instituted in February of 2006 and yet they did not sue
the hospital then.  Nor did they take it up in the two intervening amendments
to the Fitch Action.  It would appear that the possible liability of the Jewish
General simply did not dawn on the Plaintiffs' attorneys until later.  That
does not alter the commencement date of the prescriptive period.

[
258
]

As a result, prescription began to run on the claim against the
Jewish General in November 2005, i.e., less than three years before the August
2007 amendment of the Fitch Action.  Had the Court found the hospital liable,
it would have held that the claim against it was not prescribed.

O.      THE SHARING OF LIABILITY

[
259
]

Given our finding of extra-contractual liability on the part of both
doctors, and this, for the same damages, they are solidarily liable towards the
Trossmans
[66]
.  It is irrelevant that they were sued in different court files,
since the cases were ordered joined for purposes of the hearing
[67]
.

[
260
]

Where solidarity occurs, the Code of Civil Procedure requires us to
determine each one's share in the damages, where the evidence permits
[68]
.  Since we have full proof of all factual aspects of the files, the
evidence does indeed permit us to make such a determination here and we are of
the view that Dr. Watters should bear three fourths of the damages and Dr.
Fitch one fourth.

[
261
]

Dr. Watters played a larger and more senior role in this matter.  He
acted as the attending physician on several of Corey's admissions to the
Childrens.  He examined Corey a number of times over some three years.  He
discovered the diagnosis of his illness.  Dr. Fitch participated in none of
this.

[
262
]

We do not say that her role was unimportant.  She accompanied Frank
to the Childrens on one occasion and organized the research on the Article and
the access to the Uncles' files through the Royal Vic Authorization.  She also
was the principal pen of the Article.  These elements beget her liability, but
they do not elevate her role to the level of Dr. Watters'.

[
263
]

The assessment of the respective shares of the parties in solidary
damages is, by its nature, more of an art than a science.  The judge must trust
his instincts.  Our instincts tell us that Dr. Watters must shoulder thrice as
much of the burden as Dr. Fitch.

P.       DAMAGES

[
264
]

Many of these issues were settled among the parties, so that there
remained essentially only three, albeit important, questions to answer in order
to calculate the pecuniary damages suffered by the Trossmans in relation to
Jacob's care.  They are:

a.

For what life expectancy should the damages be
calculated?

b.

Should certain child-rearing expenses be awarded
based on the differential between the cost for a healthy child and the
generally higher cost for Jacob (the "
differential
") or,
rather, on a total recovery basis, assuming that Jacob would not have been born
had the Trossmans known of the risks: the so-called "Wrongful Birth
Theory"?

c.

Are certain expenses, whether past or future,
not appropriate either in part or in whole?

Q.      LIFE EXPECTANCY

[
265
]

Only one expert testified on the likely duration of Jacob's life,
Dr. James Garbern, one of the world specialists on PMD
(Exhibit P-11)
.  His
uncontradicted opinion was that, with the type of excellent care that the
Trossmans give to Jacob, he could be expected to live into his twenties.  He
felt that 25 years was a reasonable life expectancy for the boy, although he
initially declared that he could live until 30 if he had excellent care.

[
266
]

The Plaintiffs argued, without expert support, that 15 years was a
more likely period.  In support of their argument, they pointed out, first,
that Jacob had "connatal PMD", the most severe type, second, that
certain of Dr. Garbern's writings lead to the conclusion that it is not
probable that an individual with connatal PMD would live into his twenties and,
finally, that Dr. Garbern had not examined Jacob for several years and was
unaware of certain aggravating factors in his development.  Their arguments are
compelling.

[
267
]

In a 2008 article, Dr. Garbern writes that severe PMD "
is often fatal during the first decade of
life
", that patients with connatal PMD "
usually die before the third decade of life
" and that they "
typically die of respiratory complications during childhood, but with
attentive care, they can live into the third decade of life
"
[69]
.  These statements contradict his opinion before us and are
particularly contrary to his initial figure of 30 years.

[
268
]

As for his knowledge of Jacob's particular case, Dr. Garbern had not
examined the boy since 2006.  He was unaware of a number of relevant factors
tending to indicate a decline in his health, such as the onset of seizures,
worsening spasticity, dislocation of at least one hip, lack of weight gain over
the recent period and others.  This casts a shadow on his ability to opine
accurately on the point.

[
269
]

The Court must decide what is the probable life expectancy of Jacob,
not the possible one under an assumption of ideal conditions.

[
270
]

Referring to Yochai's experience does not appear to be particularly
helpful.  He also had severe PMD and died at 18, but from an accident involving
a malfunction of his breathing equipment.  Although the proof indicates that
his condition prior to that had been stable, it is not possible to make
predictions for the future.

[
271
]

In summary, considering Dr. Garbern's writings and the excellent
care one can assume will be provided to Jacob by his parents, a life expectancy
for Jacob of twenty years seems probable and appropriate.

R.      "WRONGFUL BIRTH"

[
272
]

The unfortunate appellation of "wrongful birth" does not
refer to the same type of claim as the action for "unwanted
conception", even though in both cases it is the parents who claim
damages, rather than the child.

[
273
]

In the case of an unwanted conception, but for a fault, for example,
in a failed sterilization process, no pregnancy would have occurred and no
child would have been born
[70]
.  Since there is the creation of a life that would not otherwise
have existed, the Quebec Court of Appeal has held in one case that all the
expenses of raising that child (the "
child

rearing costs
")
may be claimed on a total recovery basis
[71]
.

[
274
]

In the case of a wrongful birth, on the other hand, the conception
is desired but, because of a failure to provide adequate medical, often
genetic, information, there occurs a "loss of opportunity to abort"
and a disabled child is born.  For such children, certain of the child rearing
costs are generally higher than usual, e.g., special schooling and camps,
equipment, home modifications, etc.  This is obviously the case here.

[
275
]

The general rules of civil law require that the defendant who causes
damage to a plaintiff is obliged to repair that damage fully.  On the other
hand, the principle of
restitutio in integrum
[72]
requires that a plaintiff should not be compensated in a way that
she finds herself in a better position than she would have found herself
otherwise.  These precepts provide the basis on which each party formulates its
vision of the damages in this file.

[
276
]

The Trossmans testified that, had they known of the genetic
implications, they would have tested for PMD and terminated the pregnancy.
Jacob would never have been born.  They thus assert that damages should be
awarded on a total recovery basis, i.e., 100% of Jacob's child rearing costs.

[
277
]

Defendants, while admitting that the child rearing costs are higher
for Jacob than for a healthy child, argue that, since the pregnancy was
desired, the Court should grant only the differential.

[
278
]

A good example of the differential is seen in the cost of
schooling.  At Jacob's special school ("
Zareinu
"), tuition is
$22,500 a year, whereas in a regular Hebrew private school it is around
$11,000.  Defendants argue that their liability should be limited to the amount
of the differential: $11,500.  The Trossmans claim the full $22,500.

[
279
]

The Court has already held that, had the Trossmans known of the
genetic implications when Marcy became pregnant with Jacob, they would have
tested for PMD and had an abortion, as she did with a later pregnancy.  Medical
science was capable of identifying the existence of PMD in an embryo or fetus
at the time Jacob was conceived and abortion was easily available.

[
280
]

Thus, since the Trossmans would have avoided the birth, their
situation is very analogous to that of an unwanted conception.  In both cases,
the couple decides not to have that baby and takes – or has already taken - the
necessary steps to avoid his coming into the world: one using sterilization and
the other abortion.  No baby is born and no child rearing costs are incurred.
The main difference appears to be in the timing of the decision
[73]
.  But that is not a determining factor.

[
281
]

Consequently, we shall analyze the Trossmans' damages in the same
way as for an unwanted conception.

[
282
]

The Court of Appeal ruled in
Cooke
[74]
that, for an
unwanted conception in the circumstances of that case, the parents are entitled
to damages equalling total recovery of child rearing costs up to the age of
majority.  This was for a healthy child, so the issue of the differential did
not arise.

[
283
]

It is also true that the Court there avoided establishing one
universal rule for assessing damages in such cases
[75]
.  Nevertheless,
in paragraph 96 they cite with approval the words of the learned trial judge
who wrote that
"(t)he
general rules of civil liability apply"
(translation)
in assessing
damages for unwanted conception.  The general rules of civil liability would
grant total recovery of child rearing costs, barring mitigating conditions, and
the Court sees nothing here that would tend to mitigate the Trossmans' claim.

[
284
]

But for the faults of Defendants, Jacob would not have been born.
His parents must now pay not only the differential resulting from his
disability, but also the usual costs of raising a son, costs that they would
not have had to bear otherwise.

[
285
]

They admit that they wanted children, two, in fact.  And they had
those two children after Jacob's birth.  They thus end up with one more child
than they planned on.  This is much the same situation that the Suite family
faced in
Cooke
.

[
286
]

The Court thus rejects the argument that the differential should be
the basis for calculation of damages in the present case.  We shall assess the
damages on a total recovery basis, where applicable, since this issue does not
affect all heads of damage
[76]
.

S.       past EXPENSES

[
287
]

The parties made admissions on the amount of past life care expenses
for Jacob to June 1, 2010.  There is disagreement over two points in this
regard:

a.

whether the full amount or the differential is
payable and

b.

how to account for the cost of nursing services
over the "
interim period
" up to the date of the present
judgment, which is the date at which "
Future Damages
" would
commence.

[
288
]

The first question is quickly answered.  Given the Court's decision
on the wrongful birth question, the amount of past expenses will be set on a
total recovery basis.

[
289
]

For the interim period, "
to simplify matters, the (Trossmans) are only claiming
the amounts for Nursing Care expenses … and do not claim the amounts for any
other expenses during that period
".
[77]
They would calculate the expenses for nursing services based on
the number of nursing hours a day granted in this judgment.  This is the
correct approach, since they should not be penalized for the delay in obtaining
a judgment.

[
290
]

On the other hand, it is not proper to apply to the past the
agreed-upon rate for the future: $47 an hour.  This rate was negotiated
amicably between the parties in order to take into account the likely increase
in such fees over the next 15 to 20 years.  It is far higher than what the
Trossmans actually paid during the interim period, which appears to have been
around $20.  Several months after the end of the trial, the parties agreed upon
that amount as the rate to apply to past nursing services.

[
291
]

As for the nursing services provided for free by the Ontario
government, being the "CCAC" services discussed below, the Trossmans'
attorneys would not deduct anything for them, basing themselves on
article 1608

of the
Civil Code
.  We analyze this issue in section S.5 below and conclude
that this article does, in fact, apply in Plaintiffs' favour.  As a result, the
value of the CCAC services will not be deducted for any period.

[
292
]

Based on the hours of nursing services a day granted herein,
including the CCAC hours received, valued at the average actual cost of nursing
services: $20, the cost of past expenses on a total recovery basis has been
calculated at $720,013
(Exhibit
P-13B-3)
[78]
.  This will form
part of the award.

T.       FUTURE EXPENSES, LOSS OF
REVENUE and non-pecuniary DAMAGES

[
293
]

As noted, most of the issues concerning future expenses have been
settled among the parties, subject to a decision on the "wrongful
birth" aspect.  The Court's position on that remains the same as for past
damages, so no more need be said in that regard.

[
294
]

There still remain 16 contested items, including Marcy's loss of
revenue, non-pecuniary damages and, finally, a dozen expenses forming part of
the life-care plan.  We shall proceed in that sequence and, concerning the
expenses, take them up in the order in which they appear in the actuarial
documents
(Exhibits P-27,
P-27A and P-13B-1A)
.  The Court communicated certain
preliminary decisions in this regard to the parties so that the actuaries could
complete final calculations.  As a result, the amounts in the above-mentioned
documents are based on the Court's findings below.

T.1 – marcy's loss of revenue

[
295
]

This heading deals not only with future loss, but also with past
loss, which was calculated up to June 1, 2010, the presumed date of judgment
[79]
.

[
296
]

It is important to understand Marcy's career path up until Jacob's
birth, at which time she was 33 years old.  She has two Master's degrees,
including an MBA.  She was a marketing specialist working with investment firms
and had moved up the ladder to a point where she was earning a salary of around
$151,283 in 2002
(Exhibit
P-13B-2)
.  It was her intention to take a four-month
maternity leave and return to work full time.  She and Andrew planned a second
child and expected to follow the same procedure.  She wanted and expected to
work "
into her sixties
".

[
297
]

On the past amount, i.e., up to June 1, 2010, the discounted present
value at May 7, 2005, the date of the action, is $1,062,464
(Exhibit P13B-2)

before income taxes.  There is disagreement over whether or not that amount
should be reduced by the income taxes that she would have had to pay on her
salary.

[
298
]

Although they agree that for future income the case law requires
that she receive the pre-tax amount, Defendants argue that the same principle
is not appropriate for past income.  They submit that she should be compensated
only for her actual out-of-pocket loss and not receive a windfall in the amount
of her income taxes.

[
299
]

The Court sees no justification in the case law to apply a rule to
pre-judgment income different from the one applying to post-judgment income.
One might well have reservations about the rule itself, given the civil law
principle of compensation for actual damages suffered, but the judgments of the
Supreme Court have effectively closed off any further debate on the issue at
this point in time
[80]
.

[
300
]

That decided, the amount of the award must take into account the
Court's finding below that Marcy could have earned 25% of her previous revenue
in spite of Jacob's problems.  Thus it is necessary to reduce the total of
$1,062,464 by that percentage, giving an award of $796,848 for loss of revenue
up to June 1, 2010.

[
301
]

The positions of the parties after that date are diametrically
opposed.  Marcy takes the position that she should not be expected to work for
financial gain ever again, arguing that her job is to care for Jacob and that
this is a full-time occupation.  Defendants maintain that, with the excellent
nursing care and other services that will be provided as a result of this
judgment, she could and should return to work immediately, and full time.

[
302
]

With respect, the Court cannot imagine how, during Jacob's life,
this woman could return full-time to the type of high-powered job she formerly
held, no matter how fine the services she is able to afford.  She is a most
devoted mother, directing a great portion of her energy and time to Jacob's
needs.  It is true that not all people would be so devoted, but that is to her
credit and she should not be penalized financially for fulfilling her parental
role in such a laudatory fashion.

[
303
]

On the other hand, she will henceforth have the security of knowing
that she can obtain first-rate assistance on all required levels.  She will
undoubtedly have to be available for Jacob's caregivers, but she will not have
to hold their hand.  This should permit her to delegate more of the
responsibility for Jacob and free up the time necessary to try to build some
sort of career, albeit probably on a part-time basis, possibly from the home
and certainly at a lower level of remuneration than she previously enjoyed.
The Court adopts this position.

[
304
]

No proof was made as to what types of part-time work would be
suitable for her in the future, or how many hours a week she could be expected
to devote to it and at what remuneration, nor, for that matter, if any
additional training might be required or the duration of any start-up period.
As a result, since Marcy will be expected to earn some income, the Court is
obliged to arbitrate an annual revenue that would be reasonably attainable in
light of all these variables and restrictions.

[
305
]

It is not unreasonable that she be expected to work half time during
Jacob's lifetime, given that he attends school six and a half hours a day.
Whether she would do this from the home or from an office is of no
consequence.  As for a rate of remuneration, it would certainly be lower than
she previously earned.  As well, it will no doubt take her a certain amount of
time, and possibly training, to get back into the professional picture.
Considering both these aspects, the Court estimates that a reasonable rate of
pay would be about half of what she used to receive.

[
306
]

Half time at half pay indicates that she could expect to earn 25% of
her former revenue, thus reducing her claim for this item by that percentage
during Jacob's lifetime, as mentioned above.

[
307
]

We must also consider what will happen after Jacob's death.  Given
his life expectancy of twenty years, Marcy can expect to be able to work full
time as of May 2022.  Since her testimony is that she wanted to work "
a full career into her sixties
", she could work full time for the final years of her career,
though certainly not at the same rate of pay as she would have earned had she
worked full time over the entire period.

[
308
]

Given the parties' disagreement, there are three components for the
Court to decide on this issue:

a.

How long will it take her to convert from half-time
to full-time employment at age 54?

b.

At what age should she be expected to stop
working?

c.

What rate of pay can she expect to earn over the
final years of her career?

[
309
]

On the first question, it seems reasonable to assume that the
conversion to full-time work will take some time.  No proof was offered on the
question, so the Court must estimate the period.  We shall assume that it will
take one year, admitting that this might be somewhat generous in favour of
Marcy.

[
310
]

As to the age at which Marcy should be expected to stop working,
basing themselves on Quebec jurisprudence and workmen's compensation practices,
Plaintiffs assert that it is 65, while Defendants, basing themselves
principally on a 2003 Statistics Canada study, argue that it should be 60.

[
311
]

Defendants point out that Plaintiffs' analysis ignores two
significant variables concerning the age of retirement: sex and the level of
education.  From the Statistics Canada study, Defendants underline the
following points:

a.

The median retirement age for employees in the
private sector is 61.7 years of age;

b.

The median retirement age for all women in
Canada is 60 years of age;

c.

The median retirement age for women with a
university degree is 56.3 years of age;

[
312
]

In spite of the warning raised by the author Daniel Gardner that
"les statistiques doivent ici être
utilisées avec précaution
"
[81]
, the Court finds these statistics compelling and sees no reason not
to place confidence in them.  The variables of sex and level of education are
clearly not to be ignored.  The Court also notes that Mr. Gardner seems to
agree that "
the median
retirement age has decreased significantly in Canada over the last two decades,
from 64.9 in 1976-1980 to 61.0 in 1996-2000"
[82]
.

[
313
]

Considering these factors, and the fact that the one-year hiatus
that we assume between part-time and full-time work might be on the generous
side, the Court will set Marcy's expected retirement age at 60.

[
314
]

Concerning the rate of pay, the Court must estimate her expected
remuneration rate as a percentage of what she would have earned had she worked
full-time throughout her entire career.  Although we assume she would have
earned remuneration at only 50% of her "base" salary for her
part-time work during Jacob's life, the switch to full-time should alleviate
some of that disadvantage.  On the other hand, her age at that point, coupled
with the fact that she had not worked full-time for many years, will likely be
a bar to her attaining as high a rate of remuneration as she would have in an
uninterrupted career.

[
315
]

Based on these assumptions, we estimate that over the final years of
her career she will be remunerated at a rate of 75% of what she would have
earned had she worked full-time throughout her entire career.

[
316
]

Using these findings, the actuaries have calculated Marcy's loss of
revenue between June 1, 2010 and one year after Jacob's death to be $1,585,892
and her loss of revenue between then and her 60
th
birthday to be
$175,585.  Discounted to present value at May 7, 2005, this gives an award of
$1,373,988
(Exhibit P-13B-2)
.

T.2 – marcy's non-pecuniary damages

[
317
]

Several decades ago the Supreme Court set a limit on non-pecuniary
damages, which, taking inflation into account, is around $330,000 today.  This
is the maximum amount possible under Canadian law and it should be granted,
therefore, only in the most devastating, catastrophic and, by definition,
exceptional of cases.  Thus, a court must evaluate a plaintiff's condition
relative to those exceptional cases and calculate the award as a function of
that evaluation, meaning, as a percentage of $330,000.

[
318
]

The emotional burden on Marcy as a result of Jacob's condition is
and will continue to be extremely heavy.  Every aspect of her life is modelled
around providing for Jacob's well being, whether it be coordinating nursing and
therapy services, scheduling and transportation for treatments or simply trying
to make his existence as pleasant as circumstances permit.  Concern for Jacob
is her ubiquitous companion in every waking moment and her personal life
clearly suffers as a result.

[
319
]

That said, her suffering must be viewed in perspective.  She has no
pain or disability and can function normally from a physical point of view.
This is a huge advantage in comparison to many plaintiffs in these types of
cases.  It follows that her non-pecuniary damages should fall significantly
below the maximum allowable.

[
320
]

Marcy claims $250,000 under this head.  Defendants contend that
$125,000, half of the amount claimed, is an appropriate amount.

[
321
]

Marcy's general loss of enjoyment of life, many elements of which
are common to Andrew and are described below, cannot be questioned.  Another
aspect that applies particularly to her is the emotional effect of the loss of
a very promising business career.  It is not double counting to grant her
damages on this account as well as for lost revenue.  The latter in no way
compensates for the disappointment and frustration of having to turn her back
on the social pleasure and intellectual fulfilment of the type of career upon
which she had already embarked when Jacob was born.  It is an additional facet
of her loss of enjoyment of life.

[
322
]

All said, in assessing this type of damages a court is required to
arbitrate an amount after attempting to situate a plaintiff relative to the
most serious of cases.  Considering that Marcy suffers no bodily damage or
disability, we do not see how we can award her more than half of the maximum
set by the Supreme Court.  An amount of $150,000 will be awarded for this item.

T.3 – andrew's non-pecuniary
damages

[
323
]

Andrew's situation with respect to non-pecuniary damages is
different from Marcy's, yet many factors are common to both.

[
324
]

They will never have a "normal" family life.  The
attention that Jacob requires detracts from the quality and quantity of time
that they can devote to their twin daughters.  Having an overnight nurse in
Jacob's room, which is adjacent to theirs, robs them of much of the intimacy
that a married couple requires and deserves.  They cannot take the type of
family vacations and trips that they would like and that most families can
take.  They cannot enjoy family meals, with all members present.

[
325
]

There is another, rather particular aspect to consider.  Jacob can
be very difficult at times.  He cannot speak, but he has no trouble crying.
And he cries often and without apparent reason.  When he goes into a rage, he
cries so loud and for so long that it can push any person's patience to the
limit.  The parents are for the most part unable to control this behaviour and
must often simply "wait him out".

[
326
]

All this inevitably leads to a heightened level of stress in the
home and on the couple.  Although young and otherwise healthy, they are both
taking prescription medications to try to deal with that stress.

[
327
]

On the other hand, Andrew did not lose his career.  He works long
hours at a good job with good benefits, including extended health insurance
coverage so vital to providing adequate treatment for Jacob.  This concern
seriously limits his professional mobility and caused him to re-think his
career path.

[
328
]

Andrew claims $200,000 under this head.  Defendants suggest that
$75,000 is the proper assessment of his non-pecuniary damages, 60% of what they
suggest for Marcy.  The Court agrees that he should receive less than Marcy and
feels that two-thirds is the right percentage.  An amount of $100,000 will be
awarded for this item.

T.4 – AUDREY'S non-pecuniary
damages

[
329
]

Audrey has had a most difficult adult life.  Although she had Corey
with her for less than a year, she cared for Yochai for 18 years, a good part
thereof alone, without the physical help or emotional succour of his father.
Compared to Marcy and Andrew, her solitude had to make her burden all the
heavier to bear.

[
330
]

Audrey claims $150,000 under this head.  The Court sees no
justification for assessing her non-pecuniary damages at a lesser amount than
Marcy's.  Dr. Watters agrees with this principle, since he admitted the same
amount of moral damages for her as he did for Marcy: $125,000.  The Court thus
assesses her non-pecuniary damages at $150,000, although no amount will be awarded.

T.5 - NURSING SERVICES

[
331
]

There are a number of sub-questions to be resolved concerning the
provision of nursing services
[83]
:

a.

the effect of
article 1608
of the
Civil Code
;

b.

the likelihood that current assistance plans
offered by the Ontario government will continue;

c.

the need for schooling after age 18;

d.

the likelihood of extended hospital stays toward
the end of his life;

e.

the number of hours a day that the Trossmans
should be required to care for Jacob with no outside caregiver present over
three periods:

i.

school days;

ii.     weekends and statutory holidays;

iii.    extended school holidays;

f.

the percentage of the cost of a live-in nanny to
be deducted from the amount awarded for nursing care;

[
332
]

Before getting into the sub-questions, we note that there is
agreement that Jacob requires 24-hour care, both for assistance (changing
positions in bed, feeding once every four hours, changing his pyjamas and
bedding, etc.) and for surveillance, since he is prone to vomiting and, when he
does, he could choke to death.  The issue between them is whether the parents
should be expected to be left alone with him for any period of time.

[
333
]

On the first sub-question, the effect of
article 1608
of the
Civil
Code
must be determined.  It reads:

1608.
The
obligation of the debtor to pay damages to the creditor is neither reduced nor
altered by the fact that the creditor receives a prestation from a third person
as a result of the injury he has sustained, except so far as the third person
is subrogated to the rights of the creditor.

[
334
]

Plaintiffs, who have the burden of proof on the point, correctly
submit that the issue here is whether the CCAC would be legally subrogated in
the rights of the Plaintiffs as a result of a favourable judgment herein.  They
argue that such subrogation cannot occur, based on the language of the
Long
Term Care Act
[84]

of Ontario.  By that statute, the
Ontario Minister of Health is subrogated to the rights only of an "
injured person
",
being one who "
suffers
personal injuries
".  Since Marcy and Andrew
suffered no personal injuries with respect to which the Ontario government paid
any amount, Plaintiffs argue that there is no right of subrogation.

[
335
]

Several months after the end of the trial, the Court pointed out to
the parties that there appeared to be a
"gap in the proof"

(Article 292 C.C.P.)
concerning the state of Ontario law on this issue.  Both parties
were permitted to submit expert evidence on the point within a reasonable
delay.

[
336
]

On May 31, 2010, the Court received the written opinion of attorney
Richard C. Halpern
[85]
, a medical malpractice specialist and partner in the firm of
Thomson Rogers in Toronto.  He opined that the Ontario Minister of Health has
no legal right to pursue a claim for insured service provided to Jacob through
the lawsuit advanced by Jacob's parents, since they are not the
"injured person"
.  He also advised that he communicated with the Ministry's Manager
of Subrogation who advised him that
"there are no Ontario cases to date where the Minister has sought
to recover insured services in a wrongful birth case where the person in
receipt of the services is not a party to the litigation"
.

[
337
]

Given the absence of evidence to the contrary, the Court must
conclude that there is no subrogation possible in the present case and,
consequently, that article 1608 would apply so as to exclude any credit to
Defendants for the free nursing services provided by the CCAC.

[
338
]

Defendants, however, raise a second obstacle on this point.  They
counter that the real question is not whether they might be exposed to paying
twice for the CCAC services, but whether the value of those services can be
qualified as damages at all.  They argue that, since the Trossmans can only
claim for expenses they have effectively incurred or will have to incur because
of Jacob's birth, these free services are not claimable as damages by them.

[
339
]

Defendants offer no authority to support this position and, while
admitting that the factual base is accurate, the Court rejects it.  If the
value of such services were not claimable as damages,
article 1608
would serve
no purpose.  Why deal with the effect on damages of receipt of a prestation
from a third person if that free prestation is not claimable in any event?
This does not stand to reason.

[
340
]

Thus, the Court's award for nursing services will not be reduced by
any part of the value of the CCAC services.

[
341
]

On the sub-question of the likely continuation of the Ontario
government assistance plans, the government's Special Services at Home
Programme ("
SSAH
") provides some $16,000-worth of nursing
services that the Trossmans use during waking hours, while its Community Care
Access Centre ("
CCAC
") has been providing 53 hours a week of
nursing to the family to this point.

[
342
]

The Trossmans' expert ("
Belbeck
") takes the
position that, since there is no guaranty that either of these services will
continue for the duration of Jacob's life, she must assume that they will
terminate.  As such, her estimate of life care plan costs claims for 100% of
all nursing services required by Jacob, assuming that there will be no CCAC nursing
assistance provided.

[
343
]

Defendants' expert ("
Vellone
") notes that the CCAC
services have been in place for over 40 years and that it is highly unlikely
that they will terminate.  She admits, however, that the SSAH funding is
somewhat precarious and, as a result, assumes that it will not be continued.

[
344
]

Given our ruling on subrogation and article 1608, the question
becomes academic.  Nevertheless, should it be necessary one day to decide it,
the Court prefers Vellone's opinion on this point.  We recognize however, as
she does, that there is always some risk that such programmes will be
discontinued, particularly in an era of ever-more-volatile government
finances.  To take account of that, were the CCAC service to be credited to
Defendants, we would have applied a contingency of 15% of their value in favour
of Plaintiffs.

[
345
]

On the sub-question of the need for schooling after age 18, the
parties agree that Zareinu, the special school he previously attended, is the
best option for him.  The supplemental therapy that he received there is
important and should be continued.

[
346
]

The disagreement is over the age at which he should stop going to
school.  The Trossmans feel that, as of turning 18, he will be too old to be
with the much younger children at Zareinu.  Vellone is of the view that he
should stay until 21.  The school agrees to that and, in Vellone's experience,
children like Jacob generally stay in school as long as their health permits.
If he weren't in school, she adds, he should be put into day activity programmes,
but he must be 21 to be eligible for that under the Ontario Ministry of
Education rules.

[
347
]

The Court adopts Vellone's position.  The boy enjoys going to school
and it is doubtful that he would feel uncomfortable for the simple reason that
the other children are younger than he.  He will never grow to normal size or
possess normal cognitive ability.  Today, at 7 years old, he only weighs about
33 pounds.  Moreover, the therapy programmes offered at Zareinu are most
beneficial for him.

[
348
]

The Court will assume that Jacob will continue at Zareinu until his
expected death at age 20.  This is something of a fiction that we adopt
strictly for calculation purposes, since it is unlikely that he will be able to
attend school in his last days.  On the other hand, his life expectancy is but
an estimate as well, and the Court sees no contradiction in proceeding under
both assumptions.

[
349
]

On the sub-question of the likelihood of an extended hospital stay
at the end of Jacob's life, Belbeck is of the opinion that, in the last years
of Jacob's life, when his health will likely be deteriorating seriously, he
will remain in the family home but require 24-hour-a-day care by a registered
nurse ("
RN
").  In her view, therefore, the award should be
increased to cover the higher cost of an RN.

[
350
]

Vellone is also of the view that in the last one to three years of
life he will require upgraded care by an RN, as opposed to a lower level of
caregiver.  She feels, however, that he will have to be hospitalized for
certain periods of time.  This will lead to savings in attendant care in the
home and offset the higher cost of the RN's services.  As a result, no
adjustment need be made on this point.

[
351
]

The Court prefers Belbeck's opinion.  Given this family's history,
it is to be expected that the parents will do everything possible to keep Jacob
in the home, including providing for a hospital-quality environment and
services.  Although some period of hospitalization is possible, the Court
believes that this will occur only in exceptional circumstances.

[
352
]

On the sub-question of the number of hours a day that the Trossmans
should be left alone with Jacob, before dealing with the three time periods, we
must first consider the general question of whether the Trossmans should
receive an amount for outside caregivers 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.

[
353
]

The CCAC nurses provide overnight services for Jacob, starting at
11:30 p.m.  Jacob is in bed by 7:30 p.m. and the shift of the previous
caregivers ends at 9:00 p.m.  Thus, the Trossmans are alone with him for two and
one-half hours every evening, but for the most part he is sleeping.  Even with
the Trossmans' current strained resources, this appears to be the only time in
the day that either Andrew or Marcy is alone with him.

[
354
]

They find this a burden, since he has crying fits more often when he
is alone with them than when he is with an outside caregiver.  That said, only
"
a handful
" of those fits, in Andrew's words, have been serious enough to
cause choking and the Trossmans always found ways of controlling them.  It is
true that in one case they had to call Marcy's brother, who is a doctor, for
help, but that appears to be a truly exceptional incident.

[
355
]

Vellone is of the view that it is normal for parents to be alone
with their child, barring very exceptional circumstances, and she does not see
that such circumstances exist here.  The Court is of the same view
[86]
.  Things might not be perfect at all moments in the Trossman home,
but life is rarely perfect.  There is no reason for the parents not to have
sole responsibility for Jacob for short periods, particularly while he would
normally be sleeping during their waking hours.

[
356
]

We turn now to the three periods where the daily schedules differ.

[
357
]

For school days, the Trossmans claim 17.5 hours of caregiver
services, i.e., 24 hours minus the 6.5 hours Jacob is in school.  Vellone
recommends providing 12 hours of outside assistance, leaving 5.5 hours of
parental care.

[
358
]

The Court opts for 15 hours of outside care on school days, leaving
9 hours of parental care: the 6.5. hours of schooling plus the current 2.5
hours between 9 and 11:30 in the evening.  We do not see where we could
reasonably add more parental care than that.

[
359
]

Marcy and Andrew have two other children, younger than Jacob, and
they deserve and require parental attention, as well.  In the morning, Marcy
and Andrew will need to help them get off to school and, in the afternoon,
Marcy will need time to assist them with homework, to prepare food and to share
a family meal.  None of this would be possible if the parents were alone with
Jacob at those moments.  Defendants want Marcy to work, and the Court agrees,
but we must still leave her time to be a mother to her family.

[
360
]

For weekends and statutory holidays, the Trossmans claim 22 hours a
day of caregiver services, i.e., 24 hours minus two hours when Jacob is in
swimming class or other organized activities.  Vellone recommends providing 14
hours a day of outside assistance, leaving 10 hours of parental care.

[
361
]

The Court opts for 18.5 hours a day of outside care on weekends and
statutory holidays, leaving 5.5 hours of parental care: the current 2.5 hours
between 9 and 11:30 in the evening plus three additional hours.

[
362
]

It seems reasonable to extend the outings for swimming and other
activities by an hour, but certainly not up to the time suggested by Vellone.
Andrew testified that "
We
can only handle so much
", and the Court agrees.

[
363
]

For extended school holidays, the Trossmans claim 24 hours a day of
caregiver services on weekdays and 22 hours on weekends.  Vellone recommends
providing 18 hours a day of outside assistance, leaving 6 hours of parental
care.

[
364
]

The Court opts for 18.5 hours a day of outside care on extended
school holidays, leaving 5.5 hours of parental care: the current 2.5 hours
between 9 and 11:30 in the evening plus 3 additional hours.

[
365
]

This is a difficult time period to gauge because daily schedules
will vary greatly and there will be few "typical days" on which to
base an estimate.  Marcy and Andrew will be working, but will likely take their

of the summer.  Families tend to travel at Christmas and Spring Break.

[
366
]

Nevertheless, we must allot a number of hours of parental care in a
typical day.  Although the 5.5 hours of parental care seems high where both
parents are working, it should be offset to a degree by the other factors
mentioned, as well as by the fact that the pressure of school will not be
present.

]

$2,887,370
(Exhibit P-13B-1A)
, adjusted downward in Exhibit P-13B-4 for reasons that the Court

[

On the sub-question of the deduction of the cost of a live-in nanny
from the cost of nursing care, the disagreement is not over whether some
deduction should occur - the Trossmans admit that they would require one with

service would be required, while Vellone would put the monthly salary at
$1,560.

[

]

Since no proof was made on this point, the Court has little option

T.6 - CHIROPRACTOR AND MASSAGE
TREATMENTS

[

Jacob may well be small for his age, but the human back was not made
to support lifting even his weight on repeated occasions.  As a result of that

chiropractic and massage treatments for that.

[

All agree that the amount of lifting has to be reduced

[

The cost of the ceiling tracks for both floors is admitted at

[

feels that there will no longer be any need for such treatments once these

[
374

It seems logical that these treatments should eventually stop after
the installation of the lifting equipment.  In post-trial discussions, the

[

T.8 - CASE MANAGER

[

The disagreement on this issue boils down to whether Marcy requires
one or two hours a week of assistance in ordering supplies and managing nursing

[
380

T.9 – EDUCATIONAL SERVICES

[

The Court has decided that Jacob will remain at Zareinu until his
twentieth birthday.  That represents a capitalized cost of $232,729 that will

T.10 - SWIMMING POOL MEMBERSHIP

[
382

This is something of a hybrid item.  Although admitting that it
seems at first sight to be a differential issue, Defendants and Vellone argue
that it is really an all-or-nothing question because it represents a usual and
customary living expense.  All children in the Trossmans' income bracket would
have to pay this amount for swimming pool membership.  Accordingly, no amount
should be granted.

[
383

This reasoning does not go far enough.  For a healthy child,
belonging to a swimming pool is merely a sports option.  For Jacob, the Court
understands that it is, if not a necessity for his health, at least an
important part of his physical well-being.

[
384
]

That said, a healthy child would likely partake in some sporting
activity or another: hockey, soccer, baseball etc.  These cost money, too, both
for participation and for equipment and uniforms.

[
385
]

No proof was made of those amounts, but the Court feels comfortable
in assuming that they would total at least as much as is claimed here for the
pool membership.  For this reason, this head of damages is refused.

T.11 - SPECIAL NEEDS CAMP

[
386
]

This is a differential issue.  In light of our decision to award
100% of the costs of raising Jacob, we shall grant the full amount claimed,
i.e., $18,261.

T.12 – COMMUNICATION EQUIPMENT

[
387
]

The disagreement here isn't over whether Jacob ought to have the
best communication equipment possible but, rather, over what is the best that
it is possible, or eventually will be possible, for him to master.

[
388
]

Both experts admit that the Dynavox system is not only the best, but
also the most complex system available, and that Jacob is not currently capable
of using it.  Vellone advises that this type of communication equipment is
appropriate in cases of mild retardation and would be useful, for example,
where the patient is attending a regular school, or even university.

[
389
]

Belbeck does not deny Vellone's assessment of the system, but urges
us to consider what Jacob's capabilities might be in the future and to put
aside the fact that it is not appropriate for him today.  The Court is willing
to look to the future, but that future still requires a test of probability.

[
390
]

Sadly, nothing in the proof indicates that Jacob will progress
intellectually much beyond where he is today.  It appears most doubtful that he
will ever "outgrow" the equipment that Vellone proposes for him and
which he is using for the most part now.

[
391
]

The parties agree that such equipment represents a one-time
additional cost of $3,000 and that is the amount that will be awarded for this
item.

T.13 - POWER WHEEL CHAIR

[
392
]

As with the previous item, the disagreement here isn't over whether
Jacob ought to have the best mobility equipment possible but, rather, over what
is the best that he is, or eventually will be, capable of using.

[
393
]

Belbeck notes that Jacob's therapist told her that she thought that
a power wheelchair, as opposed to the manual ones that Defendants admit are
necessary, was appropriate for him and that it would give him some level of
independence and stimulation.

[
394
]

When Vellone visited the Trossman home in February 2009, she saw
that his current power wheelchair was stored in the garage.  She also reports
that Marcy told her that it was "
a big waste of money
".  She observed that,
when tested on it, Jacob was unable to control it, could not turn to one side
and seemed to take pleasure in banging into walls.  She questioned whether his
eyesight, motor controls and cognitive skills would allow him to use this type
of device in any independent – and safe - fashion.

[
395
]

The Court agrees with Vellone.  It seems inconceivable that a child
with such disabilities should ever be allowed to operate such a vehicle
independently.  The pleasure he gets out of driving it into walls must cede to
the interests of safety.

[
396
]

No amount will be awarded for this item.

T.14 - HOSPITAL BED AND MATTRESS

[
397
]

This is a differential issue.  In light of our decision to award
100% of the costs of raising Jacob, we shall grant the full amount claimed,
i.e., $9,645.

T.15 - SPECIAL CLOTHING

[
398
]

This is another hybrid item.  Although apparently a differential

clothing would in reality be no greater than the cost of designer and
popular-labelled clothing that children in the Trossmans' income bracket
normally wear, no amount should be granted.

[
399
]

The Court agrees with this reasoning and, accordingly, will refuse

T.16 - FINANCIAL MANAGER

[
400
]

In reply to the Trossmans' claim of $682,476 under this head, the
Defendants admit that "
management
fees are provided to (successful) plaintiffs who do not have the capacity or
ability to properly invest a significant sum of money provided for their future
financial requirements
"
[88]
.  They point out,
however, that no such fees should be granted here based on the fact that "
(t)he financial award in this case is
directly to the parents, and is not a claim passing through the injured infant
… The cognitive skills or abilities of Marcy or Andrew have not been damaged or
diminished as a result of the birth of Jacob.  They are both, clearly, very
intelligent and skilled individuals with business abilities and understanding
well above average
"
[89]
.

[
401
]

The case law supports this position.  In
Québec-téléphone v.
Lebrun
[90]
, the Quebec Court of Appeal held that an amount should be granted
for this only where the person is intellectually incapable of managing his own
affairs, adding that to do otherwise would not correspond to a reparation of
damage but to an improvement of the plaintiff's situation.

[
402
]

Justice Sopinka of the Supreme Court, in a common law case
[91]
, wrote that "
the
only principle that appears to be applicable is that the defendant must take
the plaintiff as he finds him, including his state of intelligence … Whether
this is low by reason of the injuries complained of or its natural state, a
management fee or an investment counselling fee should be awarded if the
plaintiff's level of intelligence is such that he is either unable to manage
his affairs of lacks the acumen to invest funds awarded for future care so as
to produce the requisite rate of return
".

[
403
]

Whether this reasoning would apply under Quebec civil law need not
be decided here.  Even applying that test, the Court would reject the claim.

[
404
]

In spite of their testimony as to their lack of experience in
financial matters, the Trossmans are far indeed from having a level of
intelligence that would render them unable to manage their affairs.  They are
highly intelligent and educated people and will have no difficulty in learning
to do what is necessary to protect the sums they will receive under this
judgment.

[

]

No amount will be awarded for this item.

Given the overall complexity of the financial aspects of this case,
it is necessary to explain certain matters that normally are taken for granted,
i.e., the date at which interest and the additional indemnity commence, which,
in turn, is normally a function of the capitalization date.

[
412
]

Concerning the capitalization date, as seen from the above analysis,
the Court has chosen to follow the guidance of the Trossmans' actuary and
discount future values to May 7, 2005, the date of the institution of the
Watters Action.  There seems to be little disagreement that, in the ordinary
course, interest and indemnity should start at the time the damages are
capitalized.  That said, the Defendants would pick the judgment date as the
moment of capitalization and, as a result of a procedural matter, point out
that there is a particular circumstance in this file that takes it out of
"the ordinary course".

[
413
]

They also argue that, whatever date is chosen, interest and
indemnity should start only as of the time when the expense was actually
incurred, since there can be no default to pay until the Plaintiffs incur the
disbursement.  They cite one of the Court's earlier judgments in support of
that position.

[
414
]

On the latter point, while recognizing the logic of Defendants'
argument in some circumstances, the Court rejects its relevance in cases where
the calculation is subject to a discounting process.  That process is meant to
account for interest earned on the amount awarded in order to arrive at a
present value at a given date to payments to be made after that date.
[93]
.  Where present value is calculated as of the time the action was
taken, as we have done here, interest and indemnity should normally run as of
then, because that is the date at which the discounted amount notionally should
have been paid.  In this manner, all amounts, subject to minor exceptions
[94]
, are treated as future amounts, thus avoiding the need to calculate
a month-by-month payment schedule for interest purposes.

[
415
]

This is the ordinary course, but it does not apply across the board
here.  Of the total amount of damages alleged, $13,364,000, over $13,000,000 of it was not claimed until October 26, 2009, when
the Trossmans re-amended their actions.  Since interest and additional indemnity
are awarded as of the date of default

only run against them as of the October 2009 amendment for the amounts added

The Court agrees.

being reduced interest in the event of a favourable judgment.  This is
generally a small price to pay for the protection afforded.
